   559	\subsection{A nonzero witness and the need for a compact cutoff}
   560	
   561	\begin{proposition}[Whole-space cutoff tests]\label{P:cutoff-boundary-tests}
   562	  If $\chi$ equals one on a nonempty open set, there is a nonzero rank-one
   563	  operator satisfying~\eqref{E:localized-finite-hypotheses} with a finite common
   564	  $C$. On the other hand, $\Lambda^{-\gamma}$ on $L^2(\R^d)$ is not compact for
   565	  any $\gamma > 0$.
   566	\end{proposition}
   567	
   568	\begin{proof}
   569	  Choose nonzero real $v,f \in C_c^\infty$ supported inside the plateau, and put
   570	  $\widetilde{v} = (\Lambda^{1/2}v,0)$ and $\widetilde{w} =
   571	  (\Lambda^{-1/2}f,0)$. Both are Schwartz. The block formulas give
   572	  $P_\chi\widetilde{v} = \widetilde{v}$ and $P_\chi^*\widetilde{w} =
   573	  \widetilde{w}$. Therefore, $Zx = \langle x,\widetilde{w}\rangle\widetilde{v}$
   574	  satisfies $P_\chi Z = Z = ZP_\chi$. Its two variances are
   575	  $\|\widetilde{w}\|^2\widetilde{v}\otimes\widetilde{v}^*$ and
   576	  $\|\widetilde{v}\|^2\widetilde{w}\otimes\widetilde{w}^*$. For any Schwartz $a$
   577	  and any $x \in H$,
   578	  \[
   579	    |\langle x,a\rangle|
   580	    =|\langle D_\gamma x,D_\gamma^{-1}a\rangle|
   581	    \le\|D_\gamma x\|\|D_\gamma^{-1}a\|.
   582	  \]
   583	  The inverse multiplier is applied only to Schwartz $a$, so it belongs to $H$.
   584	  Apply the inequality with $a = \widetilde{v},\widetilde{w}$ to obtain the two
   585	  variance bounds with
   586	  \[
   587	    C=\max\left(
   588	    \|\widetilde{w}\|^2\|D_\gamma^{-1}\widetilde{v}\|^2,
   589	    \|\widetilde{v}\|^2\|D_\gamma^{-1}\widetilde{w}\|^2\right)<\infty.
   590	  \]
   591	  This witness uses a plateau; no nonzero family is inferred for every compact
   592	  cutoff or identified with a source family.
   593	
   594	  For noncompactness, take $f$ with nonzero Gaussian Fourier transform. Then $g
   595	  = \Lambda^{-\gamma}f$ is a nonzero Schwartz function. The images of translates
   596	  of $f$ are the same translates of $g$. With $T_hg(x) = g(x-h)$, Plancherel
   597	  gives
   598	  \[
   599	    \langle T_hg,g\rangle
   600	    =\int e^{-i\xi\cdot h}|\widehat{g}(\xi)|^2\ud\xi
   601	    =c_d^{-1}\widehat{|\widehat{g}|^2}(h).
   602	  \]
   603	  This tends to zero because $|\widehat{g}|^2$ is Schwartz. Choose a large
   604	  spacing so that any two distinct translates in the resulting sequence have
   605	  image distance at least $\|g\|$. The input norms are identical, but the images
   606	  have no Cauchy subsequence. This disproves compactness. This proves
   607	  Proposition~\ref{P:cutoff-boundary-tests}.
   608	\end{proof}
   609	
   610	Thus, the choice $\chi = 1$ cannot be substituted into the compact-cutoff
   611	argument. No necessity at the Schatten endpoint $p\gamma = d$ is asserted. The
   612	results concern finite matrices and conditional finite operator sums.
   613	Coefficient localization, compact variance tails, an infinite Gaussian series
   614	and time regularity are proved in Section~\ref{S:actual-operator-driver}; source
   615	and Young identification are proved in
   616	Sections~\ref{S:source-driver-convergence}--\ref{S:constant-phase-young}. They
   617	are not consequences of the finite comparison alone.

1	\section{Covariance bounds for physically masked wave fields}
     2	\label{S:masked-covariance}
     3	
     4	We establish the covariance estimates needed for the operator construction.
     5	Throughout this section, Hypothesis~\ref{H:homog} holds, $a = \alpha_0$, and
     6	$\Gamma \ne 0$. For zero spatial covariance, the spatial spectral measures and
     7	noise variances vanish; the purely temporal estimates remain valid independently
     8	of $\Gamma$. We use the unitary Fourier transform
     9	\[
    10	  \widehat{f}(\xi) = c_d\int_{\R^d}e^{-i\xi\cdot x}f(x)\ud x,
    11	  \qquad c_d = (2\pi)^{-d/2}.
    12	\]
    13	The spectral convention in Hypothesis~\ref{H:homog} means that, for every
    14	complex Schwartz test $\varphi$,
    15	\begin{equation}\label{E:masked-spectral-convention}
    16	  \int_{\R^d}\varphi(x)\Gamma(\ud x)
    17	  = \int_{\R^d}\left(\int_{\R^d}e^{i\xi\cdot x}
    18	  \varphi(x)\ud x\right)\mu(\ud\xi).
    19	\end{equation}
    20	This is an identity of distribution pairings. We will not interchange two
    21	infinite measures in the associated oscillatory expression.
    22	
    23	A positive tempered Radon measure has polynomial mass growth. Indeed, choose a
    24	nonnegative compact smooth test that is at least one on the unit ball, and apply
    25	a defining Schwartz seminorm bound for the distribution to its dilations. Its
    26	mass on a ball of radius $R \ge 1$ is bounded by a power of $R$. Summation over
    27	dyadic shells then gives integrability of $(1+|x|)^{-N}$ for some $N$, and hence
    28	absolute integrability of every Schwartz test. These facts apply to both
    29	$\Gamma$ and $\mu$. Smooth cutoffs converge in the Schwartz topology, so these
    30	integrals agree with the tempered pairings.
    31	
    32	\subsection{Translated spectral growth and physical masks}
    33	
    34	\begin{proposition}[Translated spectral mass]\label{P:masked-spectral-growth}
    35	  Put
    36	  \[
    37	    M_\Gamma = \int_{\R^d}e^{-|x|^2/4}\Gamma(\ud x),
    38	    \qquad C_\Gamma = \frac{eM_\Gamma}{(2\sqrt{\pi})^d}.
    39	  \]
    40	  Then $0 < M_\Gamma < \infty$, and for $y \in \R^d$ and $r > 0$,
    41	  \begin{align}
    42	    \int_{\R^d}e^{-|\xi-y|^2/r^2}\mu(\ud\xi)
    43	    &= \left(\frac{r}{2\sqrt{\pi}}\right)^d
    44	    \int_{\R^d}e^{-r^2|x|^2/4}e^{-iy\cdot x}\Gamma(\ud x),
    45	    \label{E:masked-gaussian-transform}\\
    46	    0 \le \int_{\R^d}e^{-|\xi-y|^2/r^2}\mu(\ud\xi)
    47	    &\le \frac{r^\alpha M_\Gamma}{(2\sqrt{\pi})^d},
    48	    \qquad \mu(B(y,r)) \le C_\Gamma r^\alpha.
    49	    \label{E:masked-translated-ball}
    50	  \end{align}
    51	  The ball may be open or closed.
    52	\end{proposition}
    53	
    54	\begin{proof}
    55	  Temperedness gives finiteness of $M_\Gamma$. Its positivity follows from
    56	  $\Gamma \ne 0$. To check the Fourier constant, set $J(b) = \int_\R
    57	  e^{-Ax^2}e^{ibx}\ud x$ for $A > 0$. Squaring the real Gaussian integral and
    58	  using polar coordinates gives $J(0) = \sqrt{\pi/A}$. Differentiation and
    59	  integration by parts give $J'(b) = -bJ(b)/(2A)$. Therefore, $J(b) =
    60	  \sqrt{\pi/A}e^{-b^2/(4A)}$. Taking products over the coordinates gives
    61	  \[
    62	    \int_{\R^d}e^{-r^2|x|^2/4}e^{i(\xi-y)\cdot x}\ud x
    63	    = \left(\frac{2\sqrt{\pi}}r\right)^d e^{-|\xi-y|^2/r^2}.
    64	  \]
    65	  Apply~\eqref{E:masked-spectral-convention} to the single Schwartz test
    66	  $e^{-r^2|x|^2/4}e^{-iy\cdot x}$ to obtain \eqref{E:masked-gaussian-transform}.
    67	  Its left side is nonnegative. Taking the absolute value on the right removes
    68	  the complex phase because $\Gamma$ is nonnegative. The pushforward of $\Gamma$
    69	  by $x \mapsto rx$ assigns mass $r^{\alpha-d}\Gamma(A)$ to a Borel set $A$.
    70	  Thus,
    71	  \[
    72	    \int e^{-r^2|x|^2/4}\Gamma(\ud x) = r^{\alpha-d}M_\Gamma.
    73	  \]
    74	  This proves the Gaussian bound. On either ball $B(y,r)$ the integrand
    75	  $e^{-|\xi-y|^2/r^2}$ is at least $e^{-1}$, proving the mass bound. This proves
    76	  Proposition~\ref{P:masked-spectral-growth}.
    77	\end{proof}
    78	
    79	Choose and fix a real nonzero Schwartz function $\zeta$. For $R > 0$ put
    80	$\zeta_R(x) = \zeta(x/R)$, $k_R = \widehat{\zeta_R}$ and $L =
    81	\|\widehat{\zeta}\|_1$. Then $k_R(u) = R^d\widehat{\zeta}(Ru)$ and $\|k_R\|_1 =
    82	L > 0$. Define
    83	\begin{equation}\label{E:masked-auxiliary-measure}
    84	  \nu_R(\ud\eta) = \rho_R(\eta)\ud\eta,
    85	  \qquad \rho_R(\eta) = c_d^2L\int |k_R(\xi-\eta)|\mu(\ud\xi).
    86	\end{equation}
    87	
    88	\begin{proposition}[Auxiliary mask norm]\label{P:masked-auxiliary-norm}
    89	  The measure $\nu_R$ is even, tempered and Radon, with
    90	  \begin{equation}\label{E:masked-auxiliary-growth}
    91	    \nu_R(B(y,r)) \le c_d^2L^2C_\Gamma r^\alpha
    92	  \end{equation}
    93	  for all $y \in \R^d$ and $r > 0$, uniformly in $R > 0$. If $H$ is a separable
    94	  complex Hilbert space and $F$ is an $H$-valued Schwartz function, then
    95	  \begin{equation}\label{E:masked-hilbert-fourier}
    96	    \int \|\widehat{\zeta_RF}(\xi)\|_H^2\mu(\ud\xi)
    97	    \le \int \|\widehat{F}(\eta)\|_H^2\nu_R(\ud\eta).
    98	  \end{equation}
    99	  For a real $H$, the same assertion holds after complexification.
   100	\end{proposition}
   101	
   102	\begin{proof}
   103	  Schwartz decay of $k_R$ and polynomial growth of $\mu$ show that
   104	  $\rho_R(\eta)$ is finite at every $\eta$. On compact sets of $\eta$, the
   105	  integrands have a common integrable bound. Dominated convergence therefore
   106	  makes $\rho_R$ continuous, and $\nu_R$ is Radon. Since $\zeta$ is real,
   107	  $k_R(-u) = \overline{k_R(u)}$. Evenness of $\mu$ gives evenness of $\rho_R$.
   108	  Tonelli's theorem gives
   109	  \[
   110	    \nu_R(B(y,r)) = c_d^2L\int |k_R(u)|\mu(B(y+u,r))\ud u.
   111	  \]
   112	  Proposition~\ref{P:masked-spectral-growth} and $\|k_R\|_1 = L$ give
   113	  \eqref{E:masked-auxiliary-growth}. Polynomial growth on centered balls proves
   114	  temperedness by the same dyadic argument as above.
   115	
   116	  Bochner Fourier integration gives
   117	  \[
   118	    \widehat{\zeta_RF}(\xi)
   119	    = c_d\int k_R(\xi-\eta)\widehat{F}(\eta)\ud\eta.
   120	  \]
   121	  For scalar Schwartz functions this follows by Fourier inversion and absolute
   122	  integrability. It follows next for finite-rank Hilbert-valued functions. For
   123	  general $F$, take projections onto the successive spans of a countable
   124	  orthonormal basis of its separable range closure. They converge pointwise in
   125	  norm. The Schwartz bounds on $F$ dominate the Fourier integrals, proving the
   126	  identity by dominated convergence. In a finite-dimensional space the full
   127	  identity projection suffices; the zero space is immediate. The triangle
   128	  inequality and weighted Cauchy--Schwarz yield
   129	  \[
   130	    \|\widehat{\zeta_RF}(\xi)\|_H^2
   131	    \le c_d^2L\int |k_R(\xi-\eta)|\|\widehat{F}(\eta)\|_H^2\ud\eta.
   132	  \]
   133	  Integrating against $\mu$ and applying Tonelli's theorem proves
   134	  \eqref{E:masked-hilbert-fourier}. Its right side is finite by Schwartz decay
   135	  and temperedness of $\nu_R$. This proves
   136	  Proposition~\ref{P:masked-auxiliary-norm}.
   137	\end{proof}

   139	\subsection{Temporal completion and the original noise}
   140	
   141	\begin{lemma}[Temporal covariance completion]\label{L:masked-time-completion}
   142	  Let $T > 0$. The form
   143	  \[
   144	    \langle f,g\rangle_a
   145	    = \int_0^T\int_0^T f(t)g(s)|t-s|^{-a}\ud t\ud s
   146	  \]
   147	  is positive semidefinite on real compact smooth tests. Its null-quotient
   148	  completion $H_a$ is separable. The inclusion of tests extends continuously
   149	  from $L^2(0,T)$, with
   150	  \begin{equation}\label{E:masked-time-schur}
   151	    \|f\|_a^2 \le \frac{2T^{1-a}}{1-a}\|f\|_2^2.
   152	  \end{equation}
   153	  In its complexification the norm is given by the same double integral with
   154	  $f(t)\overline{f(s)}$. In particular, bounded measurable amplitudes on a
   155	  subinterval, extended by zero, belong to this completion.
   156	\end{lemma}
   157	
   158	\begin{proof}
   159	  Write $\Gamma_E$ for Euler's Gamma function. Away from the null diagonal,
   160	  \[
   161	    |t-s|^{-a} = \frac1{\Gamma_E(a)}\int_0^\infty
   162	    \lambda^{a-1}e^{-\lambda|t-s|}\ud\lambda.
   163	  \]
   164	  This follows by substitution in the defining Gamma integral. Moreover,
   165	  \[
   166	    e^{-\lambda|t-s|}
   167	    = \int_{-\infty}^{\min(t,s)}2\lambda
   168	    e^{-\lambda(t-u)}e^{-\lambda(s-u)}\ud u.
   169	  \]
   170	  For each $\lambda > 0$ its quadratic form is an integral of a square. All
   171	  exchanges for compact smooth tests are absolutely integrable because the
   172	  kernel row integral is at most $2T^{1-a}/(1-a)$. The same bound and $2|xy| \le
   173	  |x|^2+|y|^2$ prove~\eqref{E:masked-time-schur}. A countable $L^2$-dense family
   174	  of compact smooth tests is consequently dense in $H_a$, proving separability.
   175	  The complex quadratic form is the sum of those of the real and imaginary
   176	  parts, since symmetry cancels the imaginary cross term. Thus, the same bound
   177	  holds after complexification. Smooth density in $L^2$, together with the Schur
   178	  bound on the absolute bilinear form, extends the inclusion and the integral
   179	  identity to $L^2$. This includes the stated interval amplitudes. This proves
   180	  Lemma~\ref{L:masked-time-completion}.
   181	\end{proof}
   182	
   183	Let $\mathcal{D}$ consist of finite sums $F(t,x) = \sum_j\tau_j(t)f_j(x)$ with
   184	real $\tau_j \in C_c^\infty(0,T)$ and real Schwartz $f_j$. These give
   185	$H_a$-valued Schwartz functions of $x$. Let $W$ denote the original real
   186	isonormal noise in~\eqref{E:cov}.
   187	
   188	\begin{proposition}[Completion on the same noise]\label{P:masked-noise-completion}
   189	  The space $\mathcal{D}$ belongs to the original test-noise completion and
   190	  \begin{equation}\label{E:masked-actual-noise-norm}
   191	    \E W(F)^2 = (2\pi)^d\int
   192	    \|\widehat{F}(\xi)\|_{H_a^{\mathbb{C}}}^2\mu(\ud\xi).
   193	  \end{equation}
   194	  Define the auxiliary seminorm
   195	  \[
   196	    N_R(F)^2 = (2\pi)^d\int
   197	    \|\widehat{F}(\eta)\|_{H_a^{\mathbb{C}}}^2\nu_R(\ud\eta).
   198	  \]
   199	  Then $F \mapsto W(\zeta_RF)$ extends as a contraction from the null-quotient
   200	  completion for $N_R$ into the original $L^2(\Omega)$. The extension is
   201	  centered and jointly Gaussian. For finitely many real $F_1,\ldots,F_m \in
   202	  \mathcal{D}$, their masked covariance matrix is bounded in positive
   203	  semidefinite order by the matrix of auxiliary inner products. This gives
   204	  covariance comparison for every finite linear Gaussian image and every convex
   205	  norm power $p \ge 1$.
   206	\end{proposition}
   207	
   208	\begin{proof}
   209	  For real spatial Schwartz $f,g$, put $h(z) = \int f(y+z)g(y)\ud y$. Fourier
   210	  inversion and Parseval give
   211	  \[
   212	    h(z) = \int e^{i\xi\cdot z}\widehat{f}(\xi)
   213	    \overline{\widehat{g}(\xi)}\ud\xi.
   214	  \]
   215	  Therefore,
   216	  \[
   217	    \int e^{i\xi\cdot z}h(z)\ud z
   218	    = (2\pi)^d\widehat{f}(-\xi)\overline{\widehat{g}(-\xi)}.
   219	  \]
   220	  Apply~\eqref{E:masked-spectral-convention} to the single test $h$ and reflect

221	  $\xi$ using evenness of $\mu$. The spatial covariance is thus
   222	  $(2\pi)^d\int\widehat{f}(\xi)\overline{\widehat{g}(\xi)}\mu(\ud\xi)$. Summing
   223	  over the finitely many temporal factors gives
   224	  \eqref{E:masked-actual-noise-norm}. Schwartz decay, temperedness and temporal
   225	  integrability justify these pairings. If $W$ is initially given only on
   226	  compact spatial tests, smooth expanding cutoffs converge in the Schwartz
   227	  topology. The spectral form is continuous in that topology, admitting
   228	  $\mathcal{D}$ in the same completion.
   229	
   230	  Proposition~\ref{P:masked-auxiliary-norm}, applied with $H =
   231	  H_a^{\mathbb{C}}$, gives $\E W(\zeta_RF)^2 \le N_R(F)^2$. It annihilates
   232	  auxiliary-null tests. An auxiliary Cauchy sequence thus gives a Cauchy
   233	  sequence of noise evaluations in $L^2(\Omega)$, proving the contraction
   234	  extension and its uniqueness. Every finite linear combination of the limits is
   235	  an $L^2$ limit of centered Gaussian variables. Their variances converge, so
   236	  their characteristic functions prove that the limits remain jointly centered
   237	  Gaussian.
   238	
   239	  For the finite family let $A$ be the covariance matrix and $B$ the auxiliary
   240	  Gram matrix. Applying the norm inequality to $\sum_i b_iF_i$ gives
   241	  $b^{\mathsf{T}}Ab \le b^{\mathsf{T}}Bb$ for every real vector $b$.
   242	  Diagonalizing $B-A$ constructs a centered Gaussian vector $Z$ of that
   243	  covariance, independent of the evaluation vector $X$, on a product space. Then
   244	  $X+Z$ has covariance $B$. Conditional Jensen gives $\E\|X\|^p \le \E\|X+Z\|^p$
   245	  for every norm and $p \ge 1$. Finite Gaussian moments ensure finiteness of
   246	  both sides. This proves Proposition~\ref{P:masked-noise-completion}.
   247	\end{proof}
   248	
   249	The auxiliary completion depends on $R$ and $\zeta$. Its construction does not
   250	define multiplication by $\zeta_R$ on the original noise quotient. Nor does the
   251	finite linear Gaussian comparison assert a covariance comparison for nonlinear
   252	wave solutions. The auxiliary and original test norms need not dominate one
   253	another. No spatial representative for every auxiliary class, nonnegative
   254	physical inverse covariance for $\nu_R$, or uniform density bound in $R$ is
   255	asserted.
   256	
   257	\begin{proposition}[A physical mask need not preserve noise-null tests]
   258	  \label{P:masked-quotient-obstruction}
   259	  In the admissible case $d = 2$, $\alpha = 1$, $0 < a < 1$ and $\Gamma =
   260	  \delta_0(\ud x_1)\ud x_2$, there is a real compact smooth mask $\zeta$ such
   261	  that no finite $C$ satisfies $\E W(\zeta F)^2 \le C\E W(F)^2$ for every
   262	  compact smooth test $F$.
   263	\end{proposition}
   264	
   265	\begin{proof}
   266	  Fourier inversion on Schwartz tests gives $\mu =
   267	  (2\pi)^{-1}\ud\xi_1\delta_0(\ud\xi_2)$ in the stated spectral convention. The
   268	  measure $\Gamma$ is nonnegative, even, positive definite and tempered, with
   269	  $\Gamma(cA) = c\Gamma(A)$. It therefore satisfies Hypothesis~\ref{H:homog}
   270	  with $\alpha = 1$. This is not spatial white noise in dimension two. For real
   271	  compact smooth $g$, its spatial covariance is, by ordinary Fubini,
   272	  \[
   273	    V(g) = \int_\R\left(\int_\R g(x_1,x_2)\ud x_2\right)^2\ud x_1.
   274	  \]
   275	  Choose real even $\chi \in C_c^\infty(\R)$ equal to one on $[-1,1]$ and zero
   276	  outside $[-2,2]$. For example, on $1 < r = |x| < 2$ use
   277	  \[
   278	    \chi(x) = \frac{e^{-1/(2-r)}}{e^{-1/(2-r)}+e^{-1/(r-1)}}.
   279	  \]
   280	  The endpoint exponentials vanish to every order, so the plateau pastes
   281	  smoothly. Let $I_\chi = \int(\chi')^2 > 0$ and $J_\chi = \int\chi^4 > 0$.
   282	  Positivity of $I_\chi$ follows because $\chi$ is not constant, and $J_\chi \ge
   283	  2$. Put $g(x) = \chi(x_1)\chi''(x_2)$ and $\zeta(x) = \chi(x_1)\chi(x_2)$.
   284	  Their unmasked marginal vanishes since $\int\chi'' = 0$, whereas integration
   285	  by parts gives the masked marginal $-I_\chi\chi(x_1)^2$. Thus, $V(g) = 0$ and
   286	  $V(\zeta g) = J_\chi I_\chi^2 > 0$. For a nonzero nonnegative $\tau \in
   287	  C_c^\infty(0,T)$, set $F(t,x) = \tau(t)g(x)$. The temporal factor
   288	  $\|\tau\|_a^2$ is finite and strictly positive because its nonnegative
   289	  integrand is positive on a set of positive two-dimensional measure.
   290	  Consequently, the full unmasked variance is zero and the masked variance is
   291	  positive. This proves Proposition~\ref{P:masked-quotient-obstruction}.
   292	\end{proof}

   294	\subsection{Temporal modulation and continuous wave factors}
   295	
   296	Write $\langle x\rangle = \sqrt{1+x^2}$. Let $I = [s,s+h] \subset [0,T]$, with
   297	$0 < h \le 1$. Norms below are those of the complexified temporal completion in
   298	Lemma~\ref{L:masked-time-completion}.
   299	
   300	\begin{lemma}[Modulated amplitudes]\label{L:masked-temporal-modulation}
   301	  Let $A \in C^1(I;\mathbb{C})$, $M = \sup_I|A|$ and $D = \sup_I|A'|$. For every
   302	  real $\omega$,
   303	  \begin{equation}\label{E:masked-temporal-modulation}
   304	    \|1_IA(t)e^{i\omega t}\|_a^2
   305	    \le C_0(a)h^{2-a}(M+hD)^2\langle h\omega\rangle^{a-1},
   306	    \qquad C_0(a) = \frac{16}{1-a}.
   307	  \end{equation}
   308	  The bound is uniform in $T,s,h,A$ and $\omega$.
   309	\end{lemma}
   310	
   311	\begin{proof}
   312	  Put $c(v) = \int_s^{s+h-v}A(u+v)\overline{A(u)}\ud u$ for $0 \le v \le h$.
   313	  Differentiation at the moving endpoint gives
   314	  \[
   315	    c'(v) = -A(s+h)\overline{A(s+h-v)}
   316	    +\int_s^{s+h-v}A'(u+v)\overline{A(u)}\ud u.
   317	  \]
   318	  Thus, $c(h) = 0$, $|c(v)| \le hM^2$ and $|c'(v)| \le M^2+hMD$. Splitting the
   319	  covariance square into its two conjugate triangles gives
   320	  \[
   321	    \|1_IA(t)e^{i\omega t}\|_a^2
   322	    = 2\operatorname{Re}\int_0^h v^{-a}e^{i\omega v}c(v)\ud v
   323	    = 2h^{2-a}\operatorname{Re}\int_0^1 y^{-a}e^{i\omega hy}f(y)\ud y,
   324	  \]
   325	  where $f(y) = c(hy)/h$. Set $K = M+hD$. Then $f(1) = 0$ and $|f|,|f'| \le
   326	  K^2$. If $K = 0$ the assertion is immediate. If $|\omega h| \le 1$, the last
   327	  integral is at most $K^2/(1-a)$ in absolute value, and $\langle\omega
   328	  h\rangle^{a-1} \ge 2^{(a-1)/2}$. The claimed constant is sufficient in this
   329	  case.
   330	
   331	  Now suppose $k = |\omega h| > 1$. On $[0,1/k]$ the integral is at most
   332	  $K^2k^{a-1}/(1-a)$. On $[1/k,1]$, integrate the exponential by parts. The
   333	  endpoint at one vanishes, while the other endpoint contributes at most
   334	  $K^2k^{a-1}$. The derivative integral, divided by $k$, is bounded by
   335	  \[
   336	    \frac{K^2}k\left(a\int_{1/k}^1 y^{-a-1}\ud y
   337	    +\int_{1/k}^1 y^{-a}\ud y\right)
   338	    \le K^2 k^{a-1}\left(1+\frac1{1-a}\right).
   339	  \]
   340	  Here $k^{-1} \le k^{a-1}$ since $a > 0$. The total is at most
   341	  $4K^2k^{a-1}/(1-a)$. Finally, $k^{a-1} \le \sqrt{2}\langle\omega
   342	  h\rangle^{a-1}$ and $8\sqrt{2} \le 16$. Including the factor $2h^{2-a}$ proves
   343	  the bound for either sign of $\omega$. This proves
   344	  Lemma~\ref{L:masked-temporal-modulation}.
   345	\end{proof}
   346	
   347	\begin{lemma}[Correlated trigonometric products]\label{L:masked-trig-products}
   348	  Let $r,\rho \ge 0$. Let $P_r$ be either $\cos(rt)$ or $\sin(rt)$, and let
   349	  $Q_\rho$ be either $\cos(\rho t)$ or $\sin(\rho t)$. With the amplitude and
   350	  constant above,
   351	  \begin{align}
   352	    \|1_IAP_rQ_\rho\|_a^2
   353	    &\le C_0(a)h^{2-a}(M+hD)^2\mathcal{Q}_h(r,\rho),
   354	    \label{E:masked-trig-products}\\
   355	    \mathcal{Q}_h(r,\rho)
   356	    &:= \langle h(r-\rho)\rangle^{a-1}
   357	    +\langle h(r+\rho)\rangle^{a-1}.
   358	    \label{E:masked-frequency-pair}
   359	  \end{align}
   360	\end{lemma}
   361	
   362	\begin{proof}
   363	  Expanding the two trigonometric factors gives four complex exponential modes
   364	  with frequencies $\sigma r+\tau\rho$, $\sigma,\tau \in \{-1,1\}$, and
   365	  coefficients of absolute value $1/4$. In a Hilbert space,
   366	  \[
   367	    \left\|\sum_j c_jv_j\right\|^2
   368	    \le \left(\sum_j|c_j|\right)\sum_j|c_j|\|v_j\|^2.
   369	  \]
   370	  The first coefficient sum is one. Apply
   371	  Lemma~\ref{L:masked-temporal-modulation} to each mode. Two frequencies have
   372	  absolute value $|r-\rho|$ and two have absolute value $r+\rho$. This gives one
   373	  half of the asserted right side, and hence the bound. Repeated or zero
   374	  frequencies are permitted; no orthogonality or independence of the modes is
   375	  used. This proves Lemma~\ref{L:masked-trig-products}.
   376	\end{proof}
   377	
   378	\begin{lemma}[Continuous sine factors]\label{L:masked-continuous-wave}
   379	  Define $c_r(t) = \cos(rt)$ and
   380	  \[
   381	    b_r(t) = \langle r\rangle\frac{\sin(rt)}r\quad(r > 0),
   382	    \qquad b_0(t) = t.
   383	  \]
   384	  For $F_r \in \{c_r,b_r\}$ and $G_\rho \in \{c_\rho,b_\rho\}$,
   385	  \begin{equation}\label{E:masked-continuous-wave}
   386	    \|1_IF_rG_\rho\|_a^2
   387	    \le C_1(a)(1+T)^4h^{2-a}\mathcal{Q}_h(r,\rho),
   388	    \qquad C_1(a) = 4\cdot3^{1-a}C_0(a).
   389	  \end{equation}
   390	\end{lemma}
   391	
   392	\begin{proof}
   393	  For $r \ge 1$, $b_r$ is a sine times a coefficient at most $\sqrt{2}$. For $0
   394	  \le r \le 1$, the fundamental theorem of calculus gives
   395	  \[
   396	    b_r(t) = t\langle r\rangle\int_0^1\cos(vrt)\ud v.
   397	  \]
   398	  This includes $r = 0$. Hence, a product $F_rG_\rho$ is a scalar coefficient of
   399	  absolute value at most two times a normalized integral of
   400	  $t^jP_{r'}(t)Q_{\rho'}(t)$, where $j \in \{0,1,2\}$ and $|r'-r|,|\rho'-\rho|
   401	  \le 1$. The integral is over zero, one or two copies of $[0,1]$; with no
   402	  averages, use a one-point probability space. Its parameter dependence is
   403	  continuous in $L^2(0,T)$ by dominated convergence.
   404	  Lemma~\ref{L:masked-time-completion} makes it continuous in $H_a$ as well.
   405	  Thus, the averages are Bochner integrals, and their $H_a$ images agree with
   406	  the pointwise averages by continuity of the inclusion. Hilbert Jensen bounds
   407	  the squared norm of an average by the average of the squared norms.
   408	
   409	  Apply Lemma~\ref{L:masked-trig-products} to each integrand with $A(t) = t^j$.
   410	  For $j = 0,1,2$, respectively, $M+hD$ is at most $1$, $T+1$ and $T^2+2T$. In
   411	  every case $(M+hD)^2 \le (1+T)^4$. For real $x,e$, the triangle inequality and
   412	  its reverse imply
   413	  \[
   414	    \frac{\langle x\rangle}{1+|e|}
   415	    \le \langle x+e\rangle \le (1+|e|)\langle x\rangle.
   416	  \]
   417	  The changes in $h(r\pm\rho)$ have magnitude at most two, since $h \le 1$.
   418	  Because $a-1 < 0$, each altered bracket to the power $a-1$ is at most
   419	  $3^{1-a}$ times the original one. Apply these comparisons, Hilbert Jensen and
   420	  the squared scalar coefficient bound four to obtain
   421	  \eqref{E:masked-continuous-wave}. This proves
   422	  Lemma~\ref{L:masked-continuous-wave}.
   423	\end{proof}
   424	
   425	These estimates concern covariance forms and temporal factors. Their application
   426	to displacement and velocity is in Section~\ref{S:wave-variance}; the subsequent
   427	operator, source and moment results require their separate proofs. They do not
   428	follow from covariance domination alone.
     1	\section{Exact scaling of the canonical solution}
     2	\label{S:exact-canonical-scaling}
     3	
     4	\begin{lemma}[Canonical law scaling]\label{L:exact-canonical-scaling}
     5	  Under Hypothesis~\ref{H:homog}, put $a = \alpha_0$, $\kappa =
     6	  (4-\alpha-a)/(3-\alpha)$, and, for $T > 0$,
     7	  \[
     8	    \delta=T^{-\kappa},\qquad
     9	    r_T=T\delta=T^{(a-1)/(3-\alpha)}.
    10	  \]
    11	  The law of $u(Tt,r_Tx)$ is the canonical expansion solution $V_\delta(t,x)$
    12	  with data $(1,0)$ of
    13	  \begin{equation}\label{E:exact-fast-equation}
    14	    \delta^2\partial_t^2V_\delta
    15	    =\Delta V_\delta+\sqrt\delta\,\W V_\delta,
    16	  \end{equation}
    17	  where $\W$ has the original covariance. In particular,
    18	  \begin{equation}\label{E:exact-moment-scaling}
    19	    T^{-\kappa}\log\E|u(T,0)|^2
    20	    =\delta\log\E|V_\delta(1,0)|^2.
    21	  \end{equation}
    22	  The assertion is equality in law; it assumes no pathwise uniqueness for a full
    23	  rough solution.
    24	\end{lemma}
    25	
    26	\begin{proof}
    27	  At positive widths, time and space dilation of the Gaussian source gives
    28	  covariance amplitude $T^{-a}r_T^{-\alpha}$. This follows distributionally from
    29	  the homogeneous Radon covariance, including spatial white noise. Its source
    30	  cutoffs transform by $K_\eta(Ts) = T^{-a}K_{\eta/T}(s)$ and
    31	  $\epsilon\mapsto\epsilon/r_T^2$; the joint maximum-time and summed-space width
    32	  laws are preserved at every vertex. The Green measure has the scaling
    33	  \[
    34	    G_d(T\tau,r_T\ud z)
    35	    =r_TG_d(\tau/\delta,\ud z).
    36	  \]
    37	  It follows from its degree $1-d$ distributional scaling, also for the sphere
    38	  measure in dimension three. Each terminal Duhamel vertex thus contributes
    39	  $Tr_T\,T^{-a/2}r_T^{-\alpha/2}$. Substitution of the displayed positive real
    40	  powers gives
    41	  \[
    42	    T^{-a/2}r_T^{2-\alpha/2}=\sqrt\delta,\qquad
    43	    T^{1-a/2}r_T^{1-\alpha/2}=\delta^{-1/2}.
    44	  \]
    45	  The Green kernel for the forcing in~\eqref{E:exact-fast-equation} is
    46	  $\delta^{-1}G_d((t-s)/\delta)$; after multiplication by $\sqrt\delta$ it gives
    47	  exactly that vertex factor. Therefore, every finite list of fixed-order
    48	  coefficients has the same joint law under the dilation, including all
    49	  self-pairings, unequal orders and empty chains. At fixed $T,r_T$, remove Green
    50	  smoothing first in dimension three, with its width divided by $r_T^2$ on the
    51	  scaled side. Lemma~\ref{L:joint-fixed-order} and the absolute $L^2$
    52	  summability in Lemma~\ref{L:vertex-crude} pass the identities to the canonical
    53	  series and its second moment. No large-time and source limit are interchanged.
    54	  This proves the law assertion and~\eqref{E:exact-moment-scaling}. This proves
    55	  Lemma~\ref{L:exact-canonical-scaling}.
    56	\end{proof}

1	\section{Gaussian enlargement and the Rayleigh comparison}
     2	\label{S:actual-gaussian-tubes}
     3	
     4	We first state the Gaussian geometry with its exact covariance scale. Let $H$ be
     5	real separable Hilbert, $W$ its given isonormal process, and $X$ a strongly
     6	measurable centered Gaussian variable in a real separable Banach space
     7	$\mathscr{B}$, with $\E\|X\|^2 < \infty$. Assume every continuous linear
     8	coordinate has the form $\ell(X) = W(k_\ell)$, $k_\ell \in H$. Fix $0 < \delta <
     9	1$ and write
    10	\begin{equation}\label{E:tube-covariance-scale}
    11	  Ch=\E[XW(h)]=\sqrt\delta\,\mathcal{M}_\delta h,\qquad
    12	  H_{\rm seen}=\overline{\operatorname{span}\{k_\ell\}},\qquad
    13	  E_0=\overline{C(H)} .
    14	\end{equation}
    15	Assume $\mathcal{M}_\delta:H \to \mathscr{B}$ is compact. All Hilbert balls
    16	below are closed.
    17	
    18	\subsection{The Wiener-space realization}
    19	
    20	\begin{proposition}[First Wiener chaos realization on the support]
    21	  \label{P:tube-wiener-realization}
    22	  The variable $X$ lies in $E_0$ almost surely, with a centered Radon Gaussian
    23	  law of full support there. Its Cameron space and norm are
    24	  \begin{equation}\label{E:tube-cameron-space}
    25	    H_{\rm CM}=C(H_{\rm seen}),\qquad
    26	    \|Ch\|_{\rm CM}=\|P_{\rm seen}h\|_H .
    27	  \end{equation}
    28	  This support triple is an abstract Wiener realization, including the
    29	  measurable-norm condition.
    30	\end{proposition}
    31	
    32	\begin{proof}
    33	  The zero law has $C = 0$ and $E_0 = \{0\}$ and is immediate. A countable
    34	  norming family exists in $\mathscr{B}^*$: choose a dense sequence on the unit
    35	  sphere and apply Hahn--Banach at each point. Approximation gives $\|x\| =
    36	  \sup_j|\ell_j(x)|$. Norms of differences from a countable dense set show that
    37	  these coordinates generate the Borel sets. Consequently, $X$ is measurable in
    38	  the completion of $\sigma(W(H))$. Fix an orthonormal basis $(e_j)$ of $H$ and
    39	  set $\mathcal{G}_j = \sigma(W(e_1),\ldots,W(e_j))$. In finite dimension these
    40	  sums and projections stabilize at the dimension. Bochner conditional
    41	  expectations need no Radon--Nikodym property here: define them first on
    42	  finite-valued simple variables using scalar conditional expectations, then
    43	  extend by the $L^2$ norm contraction. Simple approximation supplies their
    44	  scalar testing identities. Gaussian regression and the countable norming
    45	  family give
    46	  \begin{equation}\label{E:tube-finite-regression}
    47	    X_j=\E[X\mid\mathcal{G}_j]
    48	    =\sum_{l\le j}W(e_l)Ce_l,\qquad X_j\longrightarrow X
    49	    \quad\hbox{in }L^2(\mathscr{B}).
    50	  \end{equation}
    51	  To justify convergence, finite-coordinate scalar events approximate all events
    52	  in the generated sigma field: the class of events whose indicators are
    53	  approximable in $L^2$ is a monotone class containing the finite-coordinate
    54	  algebra. Approximate a Bochner variable by simple variables and use the
    55	  conditional $L^2$ contraction.
    56	
    57	  Bounded testing gives $\ell(Ch) = \langle k_\ell,h\rangle$. Thus, $\ker C =
    58	  H_{\rm seen}^\perp$, and $C$ is injective on $H_{\rm seen}$. The closed first
    59	  Wiener chaos generated by $X$ is exactly $W(H_{\rm seen})$. Its covariance
    60	  image therefore has the first Wiener chaos norm
    61	  in~\eqref{E:tube-cameron-space}; unused directions are removed by the
    62	  orthogonal projection, without an inverse covariance. This is the Cameron
    63	  image under the first Wiener chaos definition. The finite sums
    64	  in~\eqref{E:tube-finite-regression} lie in $E_0$, so $L^2$ convergence and an
    65	  almost-sure subsequence put $X$ in that closed space almost surely.
    66	  Functionals on $E_0$ extend to $\mathscr{B}$ by Hahn--Banach, so restriction
    67	  preserves the scalar laws and first chaos.
    68	
    69	  Its law is tight. For each radius $2^{-j}$ choose a finite union of balls of
    70	  mass greater than $1-\varepsilon2^{-j-1}$, using a countable cover of the
    71	  separable space. The intersection of the corresponding finite closed unions is
    72	  closed and totally bounded and has mass at least $1-\varepsilon$. Completeness
    73	  makes it compact. Metric Borel regularity on these compact sets, followed by
    74	  tightness, gives a Radon law. To prove full support, the tail $X-X_j$ is
    75	  independent of the finite Gaussian sum: every tail coordinate has label
    76	  $(I-P_j)k_\ell$, orthogonal to $e_1,\ldots,e_j$. Joint Gaussianity and
    77	  countable Borel coordinates give Banach tail independence. Given $h$ and
    78	  $\varepsilon > 0$, choose $j$ with $\|CP_jh-Ch\| < \varepsilon/3$ and
    79	  $\mathbb{P}(\|X-X_j\| < \varepsilon/3) > 0$. The finite sum has positive
    80	  probability in every ball about $CP_jh$, even if its covariance is singular:
    81	  the preimage under its finite linear map contains an open ball about the
    82	  coefficient vector of $P_jh$. Independence proves positivity of every ball
    83	  about $Ch$. Closure proves that the support is all of $E_0$.
    84	
    85	  We check the measurable norm explicitly. In $H_{\rm seen}$ put $V_j =
    86	  \operatorname{span}\{P_{\rm seen}e_l:l\le j\}$. Any finite orthonormal family
    87	  $(h_k)$ in $V_j^\perp$ is also orthogonal to $e_1,\ldots,e_j$. The same
    88	  regression and Bochner Jensen argument gives
    89	  \[
    90	    \E[X-X_j\mid W(h_k),\hbox{ all }k]
    91	    =\sum_k W(h_k)Ch_k,\qquad
    92	    \E\left\|\sum_kW(h_k)Ch_k\right\|^2
    93	    \le\E\|X-X_j\|^2 .
    94	  \]
    95	  For any $\varepsilon > 0$ choose $j$ so that the right side is less than
    96	  $\varepsilon^3$. Markov bounds the probability that this finite sum has norm
    97	  exceeding $\varepsilon$ by $\varepsilon$, uniformly over every such finite
    98	  orthonormal family. Since $C:H_{\rm seen} \to H_{\rm CM}$ is isometric, the
    99	  excluded finite-dimensional Cameron subspace is $C(V_j)$. This is the
   100	  measurable-norm tail condition for the dense Hilbert image, whose Banach
   101	  completion is $E_0$. The characteristic functional of the law is $\E
   102	  e^{i\ell(X)} = \exp(-\|k_\ell\|_H^2/2)$. These facts give the stated abstract
   103	  Wiener realization. The zero space has the direct zero-law interpretation.
   104	  This proves Proposition~\ref{P:tube-wiener-realization}.
   105	\end{proof}

   107	\subsection{Closed Gaussian enlargements and the quadratic cost}
   108	
   109	We import the set-enlargement
   110	theorem~\cite{friz.hairer:20:course}*{Theorem~11.6, p.~190}, with footnote~3 on
   111	p.~190; p.~191 supplies the following context. For an abstract Wiener space, a
   112	Borel $A$ of positive mass and its Cameron unit ball $\mathcal{K}$, it states
   113	\[
   114	  \mu((A+t\mathcal{K})^c)
   115	  \le\overline{\Phi}_{\rm N}(\widehat{a}+t),\qquad
   116	  \widehat{a}=\Phi_{\rm N}^{-1}(\mu(A)),\quad t\ge0 .
   117	\]
   118	Here $\Phi_{\rm N}$ is the standard normal distribution function; the same page
   119	gives $\overline{\Phi}_{\rm N}(y) \le e^{-y^2/2}$ for $y \ge 0$. This theorem is
   120	imported, not proved here. It concerns Gaussian input sets, not Gaussianity of a
   121	nonlinear wave. We verify Borel measurability of every enlargement we use.
   122	
   123	\begin{lemma}[Compact images and attained tube radii]
   124	  \label{L:tube-closed-geometry}
   125	  Suppose the law of $X$ is nonzero and put
   126	  \[
   127	    b_\delta=2\E\|X\|,\qquad
   128	    A_\delta=\{x\in E_0:\|x\|\le b_\delta\},\qquad
   129	    \mathcal{T}_r=A_\delta+\mathcal{M}_\delta(\overline{B}_H(r)).
   130	  \]
   131	  Every $\mathcal{T}_r$ is closed. The extended distance $d_\delta(x) =
   132	  \inf\{r\ge0:x\in\mathcal{T}_r\}$ satisfies
   133	  \begin{equation}\label{E:tube-attained-radius}
   134	    \{d_\delta\le r\}=\mathcal{T}_r,\qquad
   135	    \mathbb{P}(d_\delta(X)>r)\le e^{-r^2/(2\delta)},\quad r\ge0 .
   136	  \end{equation}
   137	  In particular, $d_\delta$ is lower semicontinuous and finite almost surely.
   138	\end{lemma}
   139	
   140	\begin{proof}
   141	  A compact map from a separable Hilbert space sends a closed bounded ball to a
   142	  compact set, including closedness of the image. Indeed, diagonal orthonormal
   143	  coordinates and Fatou give a weakly convergent subsequence of any bounded
   144	  sequence, with limit still in the ball. Compactness gives norm-convergent
   145	  image subsequences, and bounded scalar testing identifies every limit with the
   146	  image of that weak limit. This proves sequential compactness. Closed
   147	  $A_\delta$ plus a compact image is closed: along a converging sequence of
   148	  sums, extract the compact component and pass the residual into the closed base
   149	  set.
   150	
   151	  Membership in $\mathcal{T}_r$ implies $d_\delta \le r$. Conversely, if
   152	  $d_\delta(x) \le r$, choose $h_j$ with $\|h_j\| \le r+1/j$ and
   153	  $x-\mathcal{M}_\delta h_j \in A_\delta$. A weak subsequence has limit $h$ of

   180	\begin{proposition}[Comparison with the Rayleigh integral, including jumps and zero law]
   181	  \label{P:tube-rayleigh-transfer}
   182	  Let $F:E_0 \to \R$ be Borel and let $G:[0,\infty) \to \R$ be Borel and
   183	  nondecreasing. If $F(x) \le G(r)$ for every $x \in \mathcal{T}_r$ and every $r
   184	  \ge 0$, then
   185	  \begin{equation}\label{E:tube-rayleigh-transfer}
   186	    \E e^{F(X)/\delta}
   187	    \le\int_0^\infty\frac r\delta
   188	    \exp\left(\frac{G(r)-r^2/2}{\delta}\right)\ud r .
   189	  \end{equation}
   190	  For zero law use $E_0 = \{0\}$, $C = \mathcal{M}_\delta = 0$; the same
   191	  conclusion holds when $F(0) \le G(0)$.
   192	\end{proposition}
   193	
   194	\begin{proof}
   195	  The auxiliary Rayleigh variable $\mathcal{R}_\delta$ with density
   196	  $(r/\delta)e^{-r^2/(2\delta)}$, $r > 0$, has mass one and survival function
   197	  $e^{-r^2/(2\delta)}$ by direct integration. It is a scalar stochastic
   198	  dominator, not a norm of a Gaussian variable in the covariance Hilbert space.
   199	  For every level $t \ge 0$, the upper level set of $e^{G(r)/\delta}$ is an
   200	  upper interval, possibly empty or the whole halfline. An open endpoint is
   201	  controlled by~\eqref{E:tube-attained-radius}. At a positive closed endpoint
   202	  $c$, let $s\uparrow c$:
   203	  \[
   204	    \mathbb{P}(d_\delta(X)\ge c)
   205	    =\lim_{s\uparrow c}\mathbb{P}(d_\delta(X)>s)
   206	    \le e^{-c^2/(2\delta)}
   207	    =\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{R}_\delta\ge c).
   208	  \]
   209	  Rayleigh has no atoms, and at the closed endpoint zero both probability bounds
   210	  are one. On the null event $\{d_\delta(X)=\infty\}$ define
   211	  $e^{G(d_\delta(X))/\delta}$ to be one. No value of $G$ at infinity is needed
   212	  and no expectation changes. Layer cake and Tonelli therefore order the
   213	  expectations of $e^{G(d_\delta(X))/\delta}$ and
   214	  $e^{G(\mathcal{R}_\delta)/\delta}$, even when $G$ jumps or expectations are
   215	  infinite. Least-radius attainment gives $F(X) \le G(d_\delta(X))$ almost
   216	  surely. No measurable selection of a control or residual is needed. This
   217	  proves~\eqref{E:tube-rayleigh-transfer}. For zero law, $X = 0$ and $F(0) \le
   218	  G(0) \le G(r)$; normalization of the Rayleigh density proves the claim
   219	  directly. In particular, $F(0)$ need not be zero. This proves
   220	  Proposition~\ref{P:tube-rayleigh-transfer}.
   221	\end{proof}

   375	\begin{proposition}[Coarse tube envelope and operator moment]
   376	  \label{P:tube-coarse-envelope}
   377	  On the support $E_{0,\delta}$ let $A_\delta$ be its closed ball of radius
   378	  $b_\delta$ and put
   379	  \[
   380	    G_\delta(r)=
   381	    \sup_{\substack{a\in A_\delta\\\|\Phi\|_{H_I}\le r}}
   382	    F_\delta(a+\mathcal{M}_\delta\Phi).
   383	  \]
   384	  This is finite, nondecreasing and Borel. There is $C_{\rm env} < \infty$,
   385	  independent of $\delta$ and $R \ge 1$, such that
   386	  \begin{equation}\label{E:tube-coarse-envelope}
   387	    G_\delta(r)\le C_{\rm env}(1+b_\delta^\nu+r^\nu),\qquad
   388	    \E\|P_{\delta,E}^R(L_\delta,0)\|^2
   389	    \le\int_0^\infty\frac r\delta
   390	    e^{(G_\delta(r)-r^2/2)/\delta}\ud r .
   391	  \end{equation}
   392	\end{proposition}
   393	
   394	\begin{proof}
   395	  Put $G_B = \sup_{|v|\le B}\|S_E(v)\|$ and $C_{\rm pr} =
   396	  G_B^2[B^{1-1/r_t}+B^{1-1/r_t-\theta}]$. The lower bound $G_B \ge 1$ follows
   397	  directly from $S_E(0) = I$. Proposition~\ref{P:uniform-actual-cameron} gives
   398	  $1 \le G_B \le 3B$, $C_{\rm pr} \le 18B^{3-1/r_t}$. Its primitive estimate,
   399	  now without the covariance factor $\sqrt\delta$, gives
   400	  \begin{equation}\label{E:tube-primitive-sum}
   401	    \delta\sum_m h_m^{r_t}
   402	    \le(C_{\rm pr}C_{\rm mean})^{r_t}\|\Phi\|_{H_I}^{r_t},
   403	    \qquad h_m=\|(\mathcal{M}_\delta\Phi)_m\|_{C^\theta}.
   404	  \end{equation}
   405	  Indeed, each primitive norm is at most $C_{\rm pr}\delta^{-1/r_t}
   406	  \|\mathcal{T}_R\Phi\|_{L^{r_t}(I_m)}$. Raising to $r_t$ cancels the $\delta$
   407	  weight, and the true partition sums to the full field norm, including an empty
   408	  cell.
   409	
   410	  The generic Banach Young bound supplies $c_Y = c_Y(B,\theta) > 0$ with
   411	  $\log\|U_d(u,0)\| \le c_Y(1+\|d\|_{C^\theta}^{\nu})$ for $u \le B$. This
   412	  follows from~\eqref{E:young-upper-refined-growth}
   413	  and~\eqref{E:constant-young-growth} by $d \le 1+d^\nu$ and $(1+d)^\nu \le
   414	  2^{\nu-1}(1+d^\nu)$. It applies on $\mathcal{L}(E)$ with multiplication norm
   415	  one, without Gaussian, positivity or Hamiltonian assumptions on $d$. For $a
   416	  \in A_\delta$ put $v_m = \|a_m\|_{C^\theta}$ and $n = N+1$. Convexity and
   417	  submultiplicativity give
   418	  \[
   419	    F_\delta(a+\mathcal{M}_\delta\Phi)
   420	    \le2\delta n(\log G_B+c_Y)
   421	    +2^\nu c_Y\delta\sum_m(v_m^\nu+h_m^\nu).
   422	  \]
   423	  The upper expression is nonnegative, so it also bounds the logarithm with the
   424	  maximum at one. The exact finite weighted power-mean inequalities are
   425	  \begin{align*}
   426	    \delta\sum_m v_m^\nu
   427	    &\le(\delta n)^{1-\nu/p}\|a\|_{\delta,p}^\nu,\\
   428	    \delta\sum_m h_m^\nu
   429	    &\le(\delta n)^{1-\nu/r_t}
   430	    \left(\delta\sum_m h_m^{r_t}\right)^{\nu/r_t}.
   431	  \end{align*}

   433	  $v_m^\nu,h_m^\nu$, followed by positive powers. Zero norms and empty cells
   434	  cause no negative powers; $\delta > 0$ and $n \ge 2$, including the case $p =
   435	  \nu$. Since $\delta n \le 2/B$, these bounds and~\eqref{E:tube-primitive-sum}

   440	    D_1&=2^\nu c_Y(2/B)^{1-\nu/p},\\
   441	    D_2&=2^\nu c_Y(2/B)^{1-\nu/r_t}

   451	  with no assumption that the free endpoint norm is one. This proves
   452	  Proposition~\ref{P:tube-coarse-envelope}.
   453	\end{proof}

   455	\begin{lemma}[Exact Rayleigh tail bound]\label{L:tube-rayleigh-tail}
   456	  Suppose $G$ is Borel and $G(r) \le A_0+Cr^\nu$, $C \ge 0$, $1 < \nu < 2$. If
   457	  $M > 0$ and $4C \le M^{2-\nu}$, then
   458	  \begin{equation}\label{E:tube-rayleigh-tail}
   459	    \int_M^\infty\frac r\delta
   460	    e^{(G(r)-r^2/2)/\delta}\ud r
   461	    \le4e^{(A_0-M^2/4)/\delta}.
   462	  \end{equation}
   463	  In particular, the operator-moment bound in~\eqref{E:tube-coarse-envelope} is
   464	  finite at fixed parameters.
   465	\end{lemma}

   467	\begin{proof}
   468	  The finite scalar cutoff inequality gives, for $r \ge M$, $Cr^\nu-r^2/2 \le
   469	  -M^2/8-r^2/8$. Its exact conditions are $M > 0$, $r \ge M$, $C \ge 0$, $1 <
   470	  \nu < 2$ and $4C \le M^{2-\nu}$. Indeed, $r^{2-\nu} \ge M^{2-\nu} \ge 4C$
   471	  gives $Cr^\nu \le r^2/4$, while $r^2 \ge M^2$ splits the remaining $-r^2/4$
   472	  into the two displayed negative terms. Analytically, $-\frac{\ud}{\ud
   473	  r}[4e^{-r^2/(8\delta)}] = (r/\delta)e^{-r^2/(8\delta)}$. Integrating gives the
   474	  front factor $4e^{-M^2/(8\delta)}$; multiplication by $e^{(A_0-M^2/8)/\delta}$
   475	  proves \eqref{E:tube-rayleigh-tail}. Such a cutoff exists since $2-\nu > 0$.
   476	  On $[0,M]$ the growth bound gives $G(r) \le A_0+CM^\nu$, so the integral is
   477	  finite there as well. Apply this to $A_0 = C_{\rm env}(1+b_\delta^\nu)$ and $C
   478	  = C_{\rm env}$ in the preceding proposition. No infinite-dimensional Gaussian
   479	  density is used. This proves Lemma~\ref{L:tube-rayleigh-tail}.
   480	\end{proof}

    54	  $L^2(I;G)$; the same bound on differences extends $J_G$. Absolute bilinear

   108	  makes no simultaneous-version assertion over all rough controls. This proves

   157	\begin{lemma}[Uniform optimizer norm and positive smoothing]
   158	  \label{L:positive-uniform-optimizer}

   160	  restricted to $\|\Phi\| \le M$, uniformly in $R$. For every finite trial
   161	  family in Lemma~\ref{L:positive-physical-gram}, the unmasked finite
   162	  variational expression has a maximizer $\Phi_D$ with $\|\Phi_D\| \le M$. It is

   164	  case it is approximable in $H_I$ by tests in $\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{pos}}$.

   169	  Proposition~\ref{P:uniform-rate-averaging} gives
   170	  \[
   171	    2\operatorname{Rate}_R(\Phi)-q^2/2
   172	    \le2+2Cq-q^2/2<2-2q<0\quad(q>M).
   173	  \]
   174	  The zero control gives zero, proving the restriction.
   175	
   176	  Denote the finite unmasked objective by $\mathfrak{F}_D$.
   177	  Proposition~\ref{P:gram-positive-optimizer} supplies an attained maximum at
   178	  zero or a positive conic sum $\Phi_D$. Choose a finite $R' \ge 1$ whose
   179	  plateau contains all supports of $f_i$. Then $k_i^{R'} = k_i^\infty$. Write
   180	  $W_i = \ell_i^{-1}\int_{I_i}\mathcal{T}_{R'}\Phi(s)\ud s$. The row identity
   181	  and real Rayleigh formula imply, for every $\Phi$,
   182	  \begin{align*}
   183	    \mathfrak{F}_D(\Phi)
   184	    &\le2\sum_i\ell_i\lambda(W_i)-q^2/2\\
   185	    &\le2+2\sum_i\ell_i\|W_i\|-q^2/2
   186	    \le2+2Cq-q^2/2 .
   187	  \end{align*}

   189	  form of the Bochner average is the average form. Here $\lambda(L) \le
   190	  \max(1,\|L\|) \le 1+\|L\|$, the norm of an average is bounded by the average
   191	  norm, and the $L^1$ mean norm is at most its $L^r$ norm. No time-averaging
   192	  error or concavity of the positive-part square root enters this estimate.

   194	  radius $M$, independently of the partition, profiles and $R'$.

   196	  On a nonzero branch write $\Phi_D = \sum_{i\in A}w_i h_i\otimes f_i^2$, with

   198	  approximate identity, and multiply by smooth cutoffs $0 \le \chi_j \le 1$

206	  Thus, $\Psi_j \ne 0$ eventually, so $\Psi_j \in \mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{pos}}$.

   208	  Proposition~\ref{P:uniform-rate-averaging} gives

   331	\begin{theorem}[Intrinsic original second-moment constant]
   332	  \label{T:intrinsic-second-moment}
   333	  For every original admissible model with data $(1,0)$ and fixed $x$,
   334	  \begin{equation}\label{E:intrinsic-second-moment-limit}
   335	    \lim_{T\to\infty}T^{-(4-\alpha-a)/(3-\alpha)}
   336	    \log\E|u_\Gamma(T,x)|^2
   337	    =C_2(\Gamma,a)=S_2^{\mathrm{pos}}
   338	    =2^{(4-\alpha)/(3-\alpha)}S_1^{\mathrm{pos}}.
   339	  \end{equation}
   340	  Its complete variational formula over nonnegative controls is
   341	  \begin{align}
   342	    C_2(\Gamma,a)
   343	    &=\sup_{\Psi\in\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{pos}}}
   344	    \left\{2\int_I
   345	    \sqrt{\sup_{\substack{f\in H^1(\R^d;\R)\\\|f\|_2=1}}
   346	    \left(\int h_{\Psi,s}f^2-\|\nabla f\|_2^2\right)}
   347	    \ud s-\frac{v_\Psi}{2}\right\},
   348	    \label{E:intrinsic-positive-formula}\\
   349	    h_{\Psi,s}(x)
   350	    &=\int_I|s-t|^{-a}(\Gamma*\Psi_t)(x)\ud t,\qquad
   351	    v_\Psi=\int_{I\times\R^d}\Psi(s,x)h_{\Psi,s}(x)\ud x\ud s.
   352	    \notag
   353	  \end{align}
   354	  Here $\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{pos}}$ consists of all nonzero nonnegative real
   355	  $C_c^\infty(I\times\R^d)$ tests, including nonseparable ones. The covariance
   356	  retains its amplitude, the kinetic term has coefficient one, and the Gaussian
   357	  action is $v_\Psi/2$. For nonzero covariance $0 < C_2 < \infty$. For $\Gamma =
   358	  0$ the constant and moment rate are zero.
   359	\end{theorem}

   361	\begin{proof}

   363	  followed by Proposition~\ref{P:positive-score-cutoff} with $R =
   364	  \delta^{-1}+2$, bounds the original point limsup by $S_2^{\mathrm{pos}}$.
   365	  Proposition~\ref{P:variational-positive-scores} bounds the original point
   366	  liminf below by this same value. Both are for the same canonical Stratonovich
   367	  solution, exponent, original covariance and variance-half action. Their with
   368	  the regularization removed first identifications retain all mixed, unequal,
   369	  self and empty chains and both phase components with initial data $(1,0)$. The
   370	  original spatial stationarity proved in
   371	  Proposition~\ref{P:raw-block-original-lower} extends both bounds to every

   374	  Proposition~\ref{P:variational-positive-scores}.
   375	  Formula~\eqref{E:variational-real-rayleigh} and the definition of the original

   378	  If $\Gamma = 0$, $H_I = \{0\}$, all means, variances and rates vanish,

   124	  $\mathcal{O}$ and has positive $A$ by Proposition~\ref{P:spatial-four-linear}.

   100	  the statewise integral $\int_0^t S_E(-r)B(mgY_{\rm fast}(r))S_E(r)\ud r$.
   101	  Fubini uses $\E|ZY| \le \|Z\|_2\|Y\|_2$ when Gaussian testing is needed.
   102	  Countable dense states, rational times and continuity give the full
   103	  ordinary-primitive identity, as in
   104	  Proposition~\ref{P:source-ordinary-response}.
   105	  Lemma~\ref{L:constant-source-solution} and
   106	  Proposition~\ref{P:symplectic-source} then identify the Young equation with
   107	  the ordinary interaction equation on $E$.

   109	  In the temporal kernel $K_\tau(v) = \Gamma_{\rm E}(a)^{-1}
   110	  \int_0^{\tau^{-1}}e^{-\lambda|v|}\lambda^{a-1}\ud\lambda$, substitution
   111	  $\lambda' = \delta\lambda$ gives
   112	  \[
   113	    \delta^aK_\tau(\delta v)=K_{\tau/\delta}(v).
   114	  \]
   115	  Hence, $gY_{\rm fast}$ has covariance
   116	  $K_{\tau/\delta}(t-s)(p_{2\epsilon}*\Gamma_\delta)(x-y)$. The shared-width
   117	  maximum and spatial heat-sum conventions persist for two sources. Positive
   118	  multiplication by $g^2$ preserves every original covariance class, including
   119	  spatial white noise. At fixed $\delta$, $(\epsilon,\tau/\delta) \to (0,0)$.
   120	  The full source point-moment limit in
   121	  Proposition~\ref{P:masked-canonical-transfer} thus applies to this
   122	  single-source law and its continuous version; no newly reconstructed auxiliary
   123	  family for $\Gamma_\delta$ is required. This proves
   124	  Lemma~\ref{L:point-fast-sources}.
   125	\end{proof}

   127	\begin{lemma}[Compact-data source identification]\label{L:point-compact-source}
   128	  For fixed $\delta,\epsilon,\tau$, the displacement $v_{\epsilon,\tau}(t,x) =
   129	  (\operatorname{pr}_1P_E^{\epsilon,\tau}(t,0)z)(x)$ has a jointly measurable
   130	  continuous version and satisfies the ordinary scalar mild equation with
   131	  coefficient $b = mgY_{\rm fast}$ and initial data $(\psi,0)$.
   132	\end{lemma}
   133	
   134	\begin{proof}
   135	  On the fixed source regularity event, $b$ is smooth in space, has common
   136	  compact support in $B_{2R}$, and is continuous in time in every bounded
   137	  spatial derivative norm on $[0,L]$. Choose integer $k > d/2+1$ and $E_k =
   138	  H^k\times H^{k-1}$. Its Bessel-unitary free matrix is
   139	  \[
   140	    \begin{pmatrix}
   141	      \cos(t|\xi|)&\langle\xi\rangle\sin(t|\xi|)/|\xi|\\
   142	      -|\xi|\sin(t|\xi|)/\langle\xi\rangle&\cos(t|\xi|)
   143	    \end{pmatrix}.
   144	  \]
   145	  The zero sine quotient is $t$; finite-horizon bounds and dominated Fourier
   146	  convergence give a strongly continuous group on $E_k$. Leibniz and the
   147	  derivative-norm equivalence, obtained by expanding $(1+|\xi|^2)^{k-1}$ and
   148	  Parseval, give
   149	  \[
   150	    \|b(t)f\|_{H^{k-1}}
   151	    \le C_k\max_{|j|\le k-1}\|\partial^jb(t)\|_\infty
   152	    \|f\|_{H^{k-1}} .
   153	  \]
   154	  Thus, $B(b(t))$ is a norm-continuous bounded force on $E_k$, with a finite
   155	  uniform sample bound $B_L$. For $Z_0 = S(t)z$ and $Z_{n+1}(t) =
   156	  \int_0^tS(t-r)B(b(r))Z_n(r)\ud r$,
   157	  \[
   158	    \sup_{t\le L}\|Z_n(t)\|_{E_k}
   159	    \le C_L^{n+1}B_L^nL^n\|z\|_{E_k}/n! .
   160	  \]
   161	  This series converges in $C_tE_k$. Iterating a homogeneous Volterra difference
   162	  proves uniqueness. Its continuous embedding into $E$ and ordinary $E$
   163	  uniqueness identify the sum with $P_E^{\epsilon,\tau}(t,0)z$.
   164	
   165	  Fourier Cauchy--Schwarz gives $\|\widehat{f}\|_1 \le \|f\|_{H^k}
   166	  (\int\langle\xi\rangle^{-2k}\ud\xi)^{1/2} < \infty$. Fourier inversion and
   167	  dominated convergence imply continuous bounded displacement, and the same
   168	  holds for velocity since $k-1 > d/2$. The source derivatives on the compact
   169	  support form a measurable $C_tC_x^{k-1}$ random element, by countable
   170	  evaluations and continuity. Picard iteration and local norm estimates make its
   171	  phase sum measurable in $C_tE_k$; the Fourier embedding gives joint
   172	  measurability. These high norms are used only at positive source widths.
   173	
   174	  The first component of Duhamel is, distributionally,
   175	  \[
   176	    v(t)=\cos(t\sqrt{-\Delta})\psi+
   177	    \int_0^t G_d(t-r)*[b(r)v(r)]\ud r .
   178	  \]
   179	  Here $G_d(h)$ is the positive Green measure of mass $h$ and support in $B_h$,
   180	  including the sphere measure for $d = 3$. The product $bv$ is continuous
   181	  compactly supported, with finite uniform $L^1$ and supremum bounds. Against a
   182	  compact smooth $\phi$, absolute Fubini is bounded by
   183	  $\int_0^t\|\phi\|_\infty\|b(r)v(r)\|_1(t-r)\ud r < \infty$. Writing $G_d(h)$
   184	  as $h$ times the dilation of its unit-time probability measure proves
   185	  continuity of the convolution term. The free term is continuous by the Fourier
   186	  embedding. Thus, the distributional identity agrees everywhere with the
   187	  pointwise continuous mild versions. No Green density in $d = 3$ or original
   188	  Sobolev point trace is used. This proves Lemma~\ref{L:point-compact-source}.
   189	\end{proof}

   191	\begin{proposition}[Cone identity and an average of squares]
   192	  \label{P:point-source-cone}
   193	  Let $u_{\epsilon,\tau}^{\rm full}$ be the unmasked source solution with
   194	  coefficient $gY_{\rm fast}$ and data $(1,0)$. At the fixed parameters, almost
   195	  surely,
   196	  \[
   197	    v_{\epsilon,\tau}=u_{\epsilon,\tau}^{\rm full}
   198	    \quad\hbox{on }\mathcal{C}=
   199	    \{(t,x):0\le t\le L,\ |x|\le1+L-t\}.
   200	  \]
   201	  Consequently,
   202	  \begin{equation}\label{E:point-source-square-average}
   203	    \E\|\operatorname{pr}_1P_E^{\epsilon,\tau}(L,0)z\|_{L^2(D)}^2
   204	    =v_d\,\E|u_{\epsilon,\tau}^{\rm full}(L,0)|^2<\infty .
   205	  \end{equation}
   206	\end{proposition}
   207	
   208	\begin{proof}
   209	  Proposition~\ref{P:masked-source-moments}, applied through the exact source
   210	  law of Lemma~\ref{L:point-fast-sources}, gives the locally continuous
   211	  measurable full solution and its $L^2$ point Picard sum. The pathwise cone
   212	  argument uses the realized pullback field; the point second moments depend
   213	  only on its Gaussian covariance through those Bochner chain sums. We place no
   214	  global unmasked field in $E$ or $F$. The cone is causally closed: a
   215	  predecessor at distance at most $t-s$ has norm at most $1+L-s$. Its spatial
   216	  projection lies a positive distance inside the plateau of both $\psi$ and $m$.
   217	
   218	  The total initial difference $(\psi-1,0)$ is represented in $E$ plus constants
   219	  by $(\psi,0)+(-1,0)$. Every entry of the full free phase kernel is a compactly
   220	  supported distribution in $B_t$, and the top-left is $\partial_tG_d(t)$. Since
   221	  $|x|+t \le 1+L = R-1$ on the cone, its entire translated kernel support lies
   222	  in the region where this total datum vanishes.
   223	  Lemma~\ref{L:constant-phase-free} therefore gives
   224	  $\cos(t\sqrt{-\Delta})\psi(x) = 1$ there. Testing the $E$ and constant
   225	  summands separately would not give this total finite-propagation statement.
   226	
   227	  The two mild equations have the same coefficient on the cone. For their
   228	  difference $w$, causal closure gives the homogeneous Green integral equation
   229	  there. Put $H = \sup_{\mathcal{C}}|w|$ and $M = \sup_{\mathcal{C}}|gY_{\rm
   230	  fast}|$, both finite sample constants. Iteration with the positive Green
   231	  measures gives $|w(t,x)| \le HM^nt^{2n}/(2n)!$. Indeed, the mass recursion is
   232	  $f_0 = 1$, $f_{n+1}(t) = \int_0^t(t-r)f_n(r)\ud r = t^{2n+2}/(2n+2)!$. The
   233	  factorial ratio forces this bound to zero on the fixed cone. No positivity of
   234	  the sample coefficient or expectation of a global source supremum is required.
   235	
   236	  At time $L$ the cone contains $D$. Tonelli and spatial stationarity of the
   237	  unmasked single-source law give~\eqref{E:point-source-square-average}.
   238	  Finiteness is the full source point-moment bound. This is an integral of
   239	  squares, not a squared average or a covariance comparison with a masked model.
   240	  Events are for each fixed $\delta,\epsilon,\tau$. This proves
   241	  Proposition~\ref{P:point-source-cone}.
   242	\end{proof}

   244	\begin{proposition}[Exact original point transfer and polynomial cost]
   245	  \label{P:original-point-transfer}
   246	  For every original model, including zero covariance,
   247	  \begin{align}
   248	    \E|u_\Gamma(T_\delta,0)|^2
   249	    &=v_d^{-1}\E\|\operatorname{pr}_1P_\delta z\|_{L^2(D)}^2,
   250	    \label{E:original-point-transfer}\\
   251	    &\le v_d^{-1}\|\psi\|_{H^{1/2}}^2\E\|P_\delta\|^2,\notag\\
   252	    \limsup_{T\to\infty}T^{-\kappa}\log\E|u_\Gamma(T,x)|^2
   253	    &\le\limsup_{\delta\downarrow0}\delta\log\E\|P_\delta\|^2
   254	    \quad\hbox{for every fixed }x .
   255	    \label{E:original-point-rate-reduction}
   256	  \end{align}
   257	\end{proposition}
   258	
   259	\begin{proof}
   260	  Assume nonzero covariance until the last paragraph, and fix $\delta$.
   261	  Equation~\eqref{E:point-source-flow-limit} gives convergence of the source
   262	  displacement in $L^2(\Omega;L^2(D))$, since $\|\operatorname{pr}_1e\|_{L^2(D)}
   263	  \le \|e\|_E$. Expected squared norms converge by Cauchy--Schwarz applied to
   264	  their difference times their sum. Separately, the full source point-moment
   265	  limit \eqref{E:masked-unmasked-moment-limit} at covariance $\Gamma_\delta$
   266	  gives convergence of the right side of~\eqref{E:point-source-square-average}
   267	  to $v_d\E|u_{\Gamma_\delta}(L,0)|^2$. Both cutoffs $(\epsilon,\tau/\delta)$
   268	  tend to zero at fixed $\delta$. Thus, the two limits in the equal prelimit
   269	  moments give
   270	  \[
   271	    \E|u_{\Gamma_\delta}(L,0)|^2
   272	    =v_d^{-1}\E\|\operatorname{pr}_1P_\delta z\|_{L^2(D)}^2 .
   273	  \]
   274	
   275	  The law normalization is the consequence of
   276	  Lemma~\ref{L:exact-canonical-scaling} and the canonical-series time change
   277	  proved in Proposition~\ref{P:raw-block-point-comparison}. Explicitly, for
   278	  $\delta = T^{-\kappa}$ and $r_T = T\delta$, $V_\delta$ has the law of
   279	  $u_\Gamma(Tt,r_Tx)$ and equation \eqref{E:exact-fast-equation}. At positive
   280	  source widths, $U(t,x) = V_\delta(\delta t,x)$ has coefficient
   281	  $\sqrt\delta\,Y_{\epsilon,\tau}(\delta t,x) = gY_{\rm fast}(t,x)$. The
   282	  fixed-order and absolutely convergent canonical-series argument passes this
   283	  time change to the point moment at fixed $\delta$. Hence,
   284	  $\E|u_\Gamma(T_\delta,0)|^2 = \E|u_{\Gamma_\delta}(L,0)|^2$. This is a
   285	  law/moment identity, not a pathwise identity on the same noise. It preserves
   286	  all mixed, unequal, self and empty Stratonovich chains and the
   287	  Green-before-noise convention in $d = 3$. The shrinking $r_T$ is not the mask
   288	  radius $R$; no spatial Jacobian occurs at point zero. The phase/operator
   289	  inequality now proves~\eqref{E:original-point-transfer}.
   290	
   291	  Parseval and the inhomogeneous Bessel weights give, for $R \ge 1$,
   292	  \[
   293	    \|\psi\|_{H^{1/2}}^2\le\|\psi\|_{H^1}^2
   294	    =R^d\|\eta\|_2^2+R^{d-2}\|\nabla\eta\|_2^2
   295	    \le C_\eta R^d,\quad C_\eta=\|\eta\|_2^2+\|\nabla\eta\|_2^2>0.
   296	  \]
   297	  This includes the negative $d-2$ power in $d = 1$. For
   298	  $\operatorname{DataPref}_\delta = v_d^{-1}C_\eta(\delta^{-1}+2)^d$,
   299	  \[
   300	    \delta\log\operatorname{DataPref}_\delta
   301	    =\delta\log(C_\eta/v_d)+d\delta[\log(1+2\delta)-\log\delta]\to0 .
   302	  \]
   303	  The nontrivial term follows by $t = -\log\delta$ and $te^{-t} \to 0$, since
   304	  $e^t \ge t^2/2$. The original point moment is at least one: its nonnegative
   305	  full pairing expansion contains the unit empty pair of chains. It is finite
   306	  by~\eqref{E:original-point-transfer} and~\eqref{E:point-fixed-finiteness}.
   307	  Thus, logs are defined without subtracting infinite quantities. Since $\alpha
   308	  < 2 < 3$, $a < 1$, we have $\kappa > 1$ and $\delta\mapsto T_\delta$ is a
   309	  decreasing bijection $(0,1) \to (1,\infty)$ with inverse $\delta =
   310	  T^{-\kappa}$. Taking logs and this change of parameter proves
   311	  \eqref{E:original-point-rate-reduction} at zero. Original canonical spatial
   312	  stationarity, proved in Proposition~\ref{P:raw-block-original-lower}, extends
   313	  it to every fixed $x$; no stationarity of the masked operator is assumed.
   314	
   315	  For zero covariance, $u = 1$, all operator paths vanish and $P_\delta =
   316	  S_E(L)$. The same total free cone argument gives the spatial-square identity.
   317	  Lemma~\ref{L:symplectic-free} gives $\|S_E(L)\| \ge 1$, and its Fourier matrix
   318	  gives $\|S_E(L)\| \le C(1+L)$. Thus, $0 \le \delta\log\|S_E(\delta^{-1})\|^2
   319	  \to 0$ and both claims hold directly without a nonzero-noise import. This
   320	  proves Proposition~\ref{P:original-point-transfer}.
   321	\end{proof}

1	\section{Finite optimization with nonnegative Gram entries}
     2	\label{S:finite-positive-gram}
     3	
     4	Let $H$ be any real Hilbert space, $\mathcal{I}$ a finite index set, $k_i \in
     5	H$, $\ell_i > 0$ and $b_i \ge 0$. Write $C_{ij} = \langle k_i,k_j\rangle$ and
     6	assume $C_{ij} \ge 0$ for every pair. The Gram matrix is symmetric and positive
     7	semidefinite, since $\sum_{i,j}a_iC_{ij}a_j = \|\sum_i a_i k_i\|^2$. Put $t_+ =
     8	\max(t,0)$ and define
     9	\begin{equation}\label{E:finite-gram-score}
    10	  \mathfrak{F}_C(\Phi)
    11	  =2\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}}\ell_i
    12	  \sqrt{(\langle\Phi,k_i\rangle-b_i)_+}-\|\Phi\|^2/2,
    13	  \qquad \mathscr{S}(C)=\sup_{\Phi\in H}\mathfrak{F}_C(\Phi).
    14	\end{equation}
    15	Let $\mathcal{J} = \{i:k_i\ne0\} = \{i:C_{ii}>0\}$. Zero vectors contribute zero
    16	because $b_i \ge 0$. Empty index sets, singular Grams and $H = \{0\}$ are
    17	allowed. For nonempty $A \subset \mathcal{J}$ and $w_i > 0$, set
    18	\begin{equation}\label{E:finite-gram-dual}
    19	  D_A^C(w)=\sum_{i\in A}\frac{\ell_i^2}{w_i}
    20	  -\sum_{i\in A}b_iw_i
    21	  +\frac12\sum_{i,j\in A}w_iC_{ij}w_j,
    22	  \qquad d_A^C=\inf_{w_i>0}D_A^C(w).
    23	\end{equation}
    24	Set $d_\varnothing^C = 0$.
    25	
    26	\begin{lemma}[Scalar and Hilbert identities]\label{L:gram-scalar-algebra}
    27	  For real $\ell$, $w > 0$ and $t \ge 0$,
    28	  \begin{equation}\label{E:gram-sqrt-dual}
    29	    2\ell\sqrt t\le\ell^2/w+wt.
    30	  \end{equation}
    31	  For $\Phi,z \in H$,
    32	  \begin{equation}\label{E:gram-hilbert-square}
    33	    \langle\Phi,z\rangle-\|\Phi\|^2/2
    34	    =\|z\|^2/2-\|\Phi-z\|^2/2\le\|z\|^2/2.
    35	  \end{equation}
    36	  For finite real $w_i$, $\|\sum_iw_ik_i\|^2 = \sum_{i,j}w_iC_{ij}w_j$.
    37	\end{lemma}
    38	
    39	\begin{proof}
    40	  Since $\sqrt w > 0$ and $\sqrt{wt} = \sqrt w\sqrt t$,
    41	  \[
    42	    0\le(\ell/\sqrt w-\sqrt{wt})^2
    43	    =\ell^2/w+wt-2\ell\sqrt t.
    44	  \]
    45	  This includes $t = 0$. If $\ell,t > 0$, equality holds for $w = \ell/\sqrt t$.
    46	  Expanding $\|\Phi-z\|^2$ proves~\eqref{E:gram-hilbert-square}. Bilinearity of
    47	  the real inner product proves the finite Gram identity. These identities use
    48	  neither compactness of a Hilbert ball nor an inverse covariance matrix. This
    49	  proves Lemma~\ref{L:gram-scalar-algebra}.
    50	\end{proof}
    51	
    52	\begin{lemma}[Interior dual minimum]\label{L:gram-dual-minimum}
    53	  Each nonempty $A \subset \mathcal{J}$ has a unique positive minimizer $w^A$ of
    54	  $D_A^C$. At this minimizer,
    55	  \begin{equation}\label{E:gram-dual-stationarity}
    56	    \sum_{j\in A}C_{ij}w_j^A-b_i
    57	    =\frac{\ell_i^2}{(w_i^A)^2}>0,\qquad i\in A.
    58	  \end{equation}
    59	\end{lemma}
    60	
    61	\begin{proof}
    62	  Put $c_i = C_{ii} > 0$ and $K_A = \sum_{i\in A}b_i^2/c_i$. Nonnegative entries
    63	  and positive weights give
    64	  \[
    65	    D_A^C(w)\ge
    66	    \sum_i\left(\ell_i^2/w_i-b_iw_i+c_iw_i^2/2\right).
    67	  \]
    68	  Completing the square in $c_iw_i^2/4-b_iw_i$ yields
    69	  \begin{equation}\label{E:gram-dual-coercivity}
    70	    D_A^C(w)\ge
    71	    \sum_i\ell_i^2/w_i+\frac14\sum_i c_iw_i^2-K_A.
    72	  \end{equation}
    73	  Thus, no coordinate can approach zero or infinity in a bounded sublevel while
    74	  a different negative term hides its growth. Take $w^0 = (1,\ldots,1)$, $d_0 =
    75	  D_A^C(w^0)$ and $L_A = d_0+K_A$. Equation~\eqref{E:gram-dual-coercivity} at
    76	  $w^0$ gives $L_A \ge \sum_i\ell_i^2+\sum_i c_i/4 > 0$. Every $w$ with
    77	  $D_A^C(w) \le d_0$ satisfies
    78	  \[
    79	    \ell_i^2/L_A\le w_i\le\sqrt{4L_A/c_i}.
    80	  \]
    81	  The sublevel is nonempty and closed inside this compact box, which lies in the
    82	  open positive orthant. A minimizing sequence chosen in the sublevel has a
    83	  convergent subsequence there. Continuity attains its infimum. Outside this
    84	  sublevel the values exceed $d_0$, so the minimum is global on the entire
    85	  positive orthant.
    86	
    87	  The function is smooth in that orthant. Its Hessian on a nonzero vector $\xi$
    88	  has value
    89	  \[
    90	    \sum_i\frac{2\ell_i^2}{w_i^3}\xi_i^2
    91	    +\sum_{i,j}\xi_iC_{ij}\xi_j>0.
    92	  \]
    93	  The first term is strictly positive and the second is a squared Hilbert norm.
    94	  Restriction to any nonconstant line segment is strictly convex, proving
    95	  uniqueness. Each coordinate permits both signs of a small perturbation at the
    96	  interior minimum. Differentiation gives $-\ell_i^2/w_i^2-b_i+\sum_jC_{ij}w_j =
    97	  0$. This is~\eqref{E:gram-dual-stationarity}. This proves
    98	  Lemma~\ref{L:gram-dual-minimum}.
    99	\end{proof}
   100	
   101	\begin{proposition}[Positive conic maximizer]\label{P:gram-positive-optimizer}
   102	  The finite real value in~\eqref{E:finite-gram-score} satisfies
   103	  \begin{equation}\label{E:gram-active-duality}
   104	    \mathscr{S}(C)=\max_{A\subset\mathcal{J}}d_A^C .
   105	  \end{equation}
   106	  If a maximizing subset is empty, $\Phi = 0$ attains the supremum. If a
   107	  maximizing subset $A$ is nonempty, a maximizer is $\Phi_A = \sum_{i\in A}w_i^A
   108	  k_i$ with strictly positive coefficients. No uniqueness of the primal
   109	  maximizer or maximizing subset is asserted.
   110	\end{proposition}
   111	
   112	\begin{proof}
   113	  For arbitrary $\Phi$, let $A(\Phi) = \{i:\langle\Phi,k_i\rangle>b_i\}$. It is
   114	  contained in $\mathcal{J}$. All other terms in the objective vanish, including
   115	  equality at the threshold. If $A(\Phi)$ is empty, $\mathfrak{F}_C(\Phi) =
   116	  -\|\Phi\|^2/2 \le 0$. Otherwise, for any positive $w$ on $A = A(\Phi)$, set
   117	  $t_i = \langle\Phi,k_i\rangle-b_i > 0$ and $z = \sum_{i\in A}w_ik_i$.
   118	  Lemma~\ref{L:gram-scalar-algebra} gives
   119	  \[
   120	    \mathfrak{F}_C(\Phi)
   121	    \le\sum_i\ell_i^2/w_i-\sum_i b_iw_i
   122	    +\langle\Phi,z\rangle-\|\Phi\|^2/2
   123	    \le D_A^C(w).
   124	  \]
   125	  This holds for every positive $w$, so $\mathfrak{F}_C(\Phi) \le d_A^C$. There
   126	  are finitely many subsets and their values are finite by
   127	  Lemma~\ref{L:gram-dual-minimum}. Taking the supremum bounds $\mathscr{S}(C)$
   128	  above by their maximum.
   129	
   130	  Conversely, $\mathfrak{F}_C(0) = 0 = d_\varnothing^C$. For nonempty $A$, take
   131	  its dual minimizer. Equation~\eqref{E:gram-dual-stationarity} makes every
   132	  vector in $A$ strictly active at $\Phi_A$, with
   133	  $\sqrt{\langle\Phi_A,k_i\rangle-b_i} = \ell_i/w_i^A$. Both inequalities in the
   134	  preceding display are then equalities for the sum restricted to $A$, since $z
   135	  = \Phi_A$. This restricted objective equals $d_A^C$. All omitted vectors
   136	  contribute nonnegative terms to the full objective, hence
   137	  $\mathfrak{F}_C(\Phi_A) \ge d_A^C$, even if this value is negative. Maximizing
   138	  over $A$, including the empty set, proves \eqref{E:gram-active-duality} and
   139	  the asserted attainment. For a maximizing nonempty subset the upper and lower
   140	  bounds force $\mathfrak{F}_C(\Phi_A) = d_A^C$; no outside inactivity was
   141	  assumed. All-zero vectors give $\mathscr{S}(C) = 0$ directly. This proves
   142	  Proposition~\ref{P:gram-positive-optimizer}.
   143	\end{proof}

   147	\begin{lemma}[Real Gram realization]\label{L:gram-realization}
   148	  Every finite real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix is the Gram matrix of
   149	  vectors in a finite-dimensional real Hilbert space. When its entries are
   150	  nonnegative, the value $\mathscr{S}(C)$ is independent of its realization.
   151	\end{lemma}
   152	
   153	\begin{proof}
   154	  Induct on the size, with the empty matrix realized in $\{0\}$. Diagonal
   155	  entries are nonnegative. If all vanish, testing on $e_i+t e_j$ gives $2tC_{ij}
   156	  \ge 0$ for every real $t$, hence $C = 0$, realized by zero vectors. Otherwise
   157	  permute a positive diagonal $c$ into the first position and write $C =
   158	  \left[\begin{smallmatrix}c&v^{\mathsf{T}}\\v&A\end{smallmatrix}\right]$. The
   159	  Schur complement $B = A-vv^{\mathsf{T}}/c$ is positive semidefinite: test the
   160	  original quadratic form on $(-v^{\mathsf{T}}y/c,y)$. Realize $B$ by vectors
   161	  $u_i$ using the induction hypothesis. Then $k_1 = (\sqrt c,0)$ and $k_i =
   162	  (v_i/\sqrt c,u_i)$ for the other indices realize $C$. Undo the permutation.
   163	  Entries of $B$ need not be nonnegative; this construction requires neither
   164	  nonnegative coordinates nor complete positivity.
   165	
   166	  In any realization, $C_{ii} = 0$ means $k_i = 0$, so its entire row vanishes.
   167	  Formula~\eqref{E:gram-active-duality} depends only on $C,\ell,b$ and these
   168	  eligible indices. It therefore proves realization independence whenever the
   169	  entries are nonnegative, which is the scope in which $\mathscr{S}(C)$ is used.
   170	  This proves Lemma~\ref{L:gram-realization}.
   171	\end{proof}
   172	
   173	\begin{proposition}[Entrywise Gram comparison]\label{P:gram-entrywise-comparison}
   174	  Let $C,D$ be real symmetric positive semidefinite matrices on the same finite
   175	  index set, with $0 \le C_{ij} \le D_{ij}$. With the same $\ell_i > 0,b_i \ge
   176	  0$,
   177	  \[
   178	    \mathscr{S}(C)\le\mathscr{S}(D).
   179	  \]
   180	  No positive-semidefinite order on $D-C$ is required.
   181	\end{proposition}
   182	
   183	\begin{proof}
   184	  Lemma~\ref{L:gram-realization} defines both values. Their eligible sets
   185	  satisfy $\mathcal{J}_C \subset \mathcal{J}_D$. For nonempty $A \subset
   186	  \mathcal{J}_C$ and positive weights,
   187	  \[
   188	    D_A^D(w)-D_A^C(w)
   189	    =\frac12\sum_{i,j\in A}w_i(D_{ij}-C_{ij})w_j\ge0.
   190	  \]
   191	  Taking infima gives $d_A^C \le d_A^D$. The empty values are both zero. Taking
   192	  maxima and using the inclusion of eligible families proves the claim by
   193	  Proposition~\ref{P:gram-positive-optimizer}. This includes the appearance of
   194	  previously zero vectors. This proves
   195	  Proposition~\ref{P:gram-entrywise-comparison}.
   196	\end{proof}
   197	
   198	\begin{remark}[Exact checks and scope]\label{R:gram-controls}
   199	  The empty value is essential: for one vector with $C = 1$, $\ell = 1/10,b =
   200	  4$, the nonempty dual has $D(4) = -3199/400 < 0$, whereas the primal objective
   201	  at zero is zero. Global concavity is unavailable: for $k = \ell = b = 1$ the
   202	  objective $2\sqrt{(\phi-1)_+}-\phi^2/2$ decreases on $[0,1]$ and has infinite
   203	  positive right slope at one. For $k = \ell = 1,b = 0$, differentiation on
   204	  $\phi > 0$ gives the maximum $3/2$ at $\phi = 1$; on $\phi \le 0$ the
   205	  objective is nonpositive. Doubling the cost changes the positive critical
   206	  point to $2^{-2/3}$ and the maximum to $3\,2^{-4/3}$. Finally, $C = I_2$, $D =
   207	  \left[\begin{smallmatrix}1&1/2\\1/2&1\end{smallmatrix}\right]$ are nonnegative
   208	  positive semidefinite Grams but $D-C$ has eigenvalues $1/2,-1/2$. These are
   209	  finite analytic checks, not a covariance-order theorem for physical waves.
   210	
   211	  The scalar, finite Gram, conditional active upper and half-quadratic entrywise
   212	  deductions have existing local Lean certificates at their exact hypotheses.
   213	  Dual coercivity, calculus, attainment, realization and the infimum/maximum
   214	  argument above remain analytic proofs. No new kernel fact or formalization of
   215	  the physical application follows merely from these certificates.
   216	\end{remark}

    28	\subsection{Uniform outer factors and the exact whole-space envelope}
    29	
    30	Fix real $\chi_0 \in C_c^\infty(\R^d)$, equal to one on $B_1$ and supported in
    31	the closed ball of radius two. Choose real $\psi_0 \in C_c^\infty(\R^d)$, equal
    32	to one on a neighbourhood of $\operatorname{supp}\chi_0$ and supported inside
    33	$B_3$. For $\rho \ge 1$ put $\chi_\rho(x) = \chi_0(x/\rho)$, $\psi_\rho(x) =
    34	\psi_0(x/\rho)$ and $L = 2\pi\rho$. Since $3 < \pi$, both cutoffs are supported
    35	strictly inside the cube of side $L$. The auxiliary torus has unnormalized
    36	$L^2(Q_L,\ud x)$, orthonormal modes $L^{-d/2}e^{ik\cdot x/\rho}$ and Sobolev
    37	weights $\langle k/\rho\rangle^r$.
    38	
    39	\begin{lemma}[Uniform rescaled outer maps]\label{L:radius-outer-maps}
    40	  The cutoff periodization and recovery maps from
    41	  Lemma~\ref{L:cutoff-factorization} satisfy, for every real $r$,
    42	  \[
    43	    \|\mathcal{P}_{\psi_\rho}:H^r(\R^d)\to H^r(\mathbb{T}_L)\|
    44	    \le C_{\psi_0,r},\qquad
    45	    \|\mathcal{E}_{\chi_\rho}:H^r(\mathbb{T}_L)\to H^r(\R^d)\|
    46	    \le C_{\chi_0,r},
    47	  \]
    48	  independently of $\rho \ge 1$.
    49	\end{lemma}
    50	
    51	\begin{proof}
    52	  The exact weighted Fourier kernels are
    53	  \begin{align*}
    54	    &L^{-d/2}
    55	    \left(\frac{\langle k/\rho\rangle}{\langle\xi\rangle}\right)^r
    56	    \widehat{\psi_\rho}(k/\rho-\xi),\\
    57	    &L^{-d/2}
    58	    \left(\frac{\langle\xi\rangle}{\langle k/\rho\rangle}\right)^r
    59	    \widehat{\chi_\rho}(\xi-k/\rho).
    60	  \end{align*}
    61	  There is no additional $(2\pi)^{-d/2}$: it cancels between Fourier inversion
    62	  and the ordinary integral in the first kernel, while the torus normalization
    63	  gives the second. For either base profile $\phi_0$, $\widehat{\phi_\rho}(t) =
    64	  \rho^d\widehat{\phi_0}(\rho t)$. Peetre's inequality~\eqref{E:cutoff-peetre},
    65	  also for negative $r$, and $\langle(\rho\xi-k)/\rho\rangle \le
    66	  \langle\rho\xi-k\rangle$ bound the relevant kernel by
    67	  \[
    68	    C_r\rho^{d/2}F_r(k-\rho\xi),\qquad
    69	    F_r(t)=|\widehat{\phi_0}(\pm t)|\langle t\rangle^{|r|}.
    70	  \]
    71	  The nonnegative $F_r$ is integrable and bounded by arbitrarily high inverse
    72	  powers of $\langle t\rangle$. At fixed $k$, integration in $\xi$ gives a bound
    73	  $C\rho^{-d/2}$. At fixed $\xi$, summation in $k$ gives $C\rho^{d/2}$:
    74	  translate $\rho\xi$ into a unit lattice cell and sum a power tail of order
    75	  greater than $d$, as in~\eqref{E:cutoff-lattice-sum}. This lattice spacing is
    76	  one and has no remaining $\rho$ dependence. The mixed Schur estimate bounds
    77	  the operator norm by the square root of the product of those two quantities.
    78	  Their radius powers cancel. For recovery the row and column roles are
    79	  reversed.
    80	
    81	  Bounded kernel extension from Schwartz functions and torus polynomials gives
    82	  the full Sobolev maps by density. Their distributional meanings are the same
    83	  cutoff maps as in Lemma~\ref{L:cutoff-factorization}; no point sampling of a
    84	  rough Fourier function is used. This includes negative indices. This proves
    85	  Lemma~\ref{L:radius-outer-maps}.
    86	\end{proof}
