    88	\begin{proposition}[Radius-explicit compact envelopes]
    89	  \label{P:radius-compact-envelopes}
    90	  For real $\sigma$, $\gamma > 0$ and $q \ge 1$ with $q\gamma > d$,
    91	  \begin{equation}\label{E:radius-cutoff-Schatten}
    92	    \|\Lambda^\sigma\chi_\rho\Lambda^{-\sigma-\gamma}\|_{S_q}
    93	    \le C_{\sigma,\gamma,q,d,\chi_0,\psi_0}\rho^{d/q}.
    94	  \end{equation}
    95	  In the balanced coordinates of~\eqref{E:compact-two-factors},
    96	  \begin{equation}\label{E:radius-two-envelopes}
    97	    \|K_{\rm in}\|_{S_q}=\|K_{\rm out}\|_{S_q}
    98	    \le C_q\rho^{d/q}.
    99	  \end{equation}
   100	\end{proposition}
   101	
   102	\begin{proof}
   103	  The exact recovery identity, with $\chi_\rho\psi_\rho = \chi_\rho$, gives
   104	  \[
   105	    \Lambda^\sigma\chi_\rho\Lambda^{-\sigma-\gamma}
   106	    =\Lambda^\sigma\mathcal{E}_{\chi_\rho}\mathcal{I}_\gamma
   107	    \mathcal{P}_{\psi_\rho}\Lambda^{-\sigma-\gamma}.
   108	  \]
   109	  Here $\mathcal{I}_\gamma:H^{\sigma+\gamma}(\mathbb{T}_L) \to
   110	  H^\sigma(\mathbb{T}_L)$ has diagonal singular values $\langle
   111	  k/\rho\rangle^{-\gamma}$. The outer Bessel maps are unitary on their indicated
   112	  Sobolev domains. The preceding lemma bounds both other outer maps uniformly in
   113	  $\rho$. This is an equality on the full whole-space domain by the recovery
   114	  proof and density, including negative $\sigma$.
   115	
   116	  Put $u = q\gamma > d$. If $x \in k+[-1/2,1/2]^d$, then
   117	  \[
   118	    \langle x/\rho\rangle
   119	    \le\sqrt2\langle k/\rho\rangle\langle(x-k)/\rho\rangle
   120	    \le c_d'\langle k/\rho\rangle,\qquad
   121	    c_d'=\sqrt{2(1+d/4)}.
   122	  \]
   123	  Integrate over the unit cubes to obtain
   124	  \begin{equation}\label{E:radius-lattice-volume}
   125	    \sum_{k\in\mathbb{Z}^d}\langle k/\rho\rangle^{-u}
   126	    \le(c_d')^u\rho^d\int_{\R^d}\langle y\rangle^{-u}\ud y
   127	    \le C_{d,u}\rho^d .
   128	  \end{equation}
   129	  The integral is finite: dyadic annuli outside the unit ball give a geometric
   130	  series with terms bounded by $C_d2^{j(d-u)}$.
   131	
   132	  Arrange the inclusion's diagonal values in decreasing order $(\lambda_j)$.
   133	  They tend to zero. Retaining its first $j-1$ coordinates has rank less than
   134	  $j$ and error $\lambda_j$. Compose this approximation with the bounded outer
   135	  factors. The singular-value approximation argument in
   136	  Proposition~\ref{P:cutoff-singular-values} gives $s_j \le
   137	  C_{\chi_0,\sigma}C_{\psi_0,\sigma+\gamma}\lambda_j$. Finite-rank approximation
   138	  also proves compactness. Summing $q$th powers and
   139	  using~\eqref{E:radius-lattice-volume} proves~\eqref{E:radius-cutoff-Schatten}.
   140	  No separate Schatten ideal theorem is needed.
   141	
   142	  The two blocks of $K_{\rm out} = P_{\chi_\rho}D_\gamma$ are the whole-space
   143	  operators with $\sigma = 1/2,-1/2$. Their $q$th power norms add, proving its
   144	  bound. Proposition~\ref{P:compact-two-envelopes} gives $K_{\rm in} = V K_{\rm
   145	  out}V$ for the unitary coordinate swap $V(z_1,z_2) = (z_2,z_1)$, so their
   146	  norms agree. In~\eqref{E:radius-anchor-parameters}, $\gamma < 1/2$ and
   147	  $q\gamma > d$ force $q > 2d \ge 2$; there is no Hilbert--Schmidt conclusion.
   148	  Neither $P_{\chi_\rho}$ nor its adjoint is assumed selfadjoint or idempotent.
   149	  This proves Proposition~\ref{P:radius-compact-envelopes}.
   150	\end{proof}

   152	\subsection{The operator path and covariance contractions}
   153	
   154	Write $M_R(W) = A_{m_R}(W)$ for the $E$ interaction operator path starting at
   155	zero on $[0,B]$ from Proposition~\ref{P:actual-operator-driver}. The phase
   156	remains the whole-space $E$ throughout.
   157	
   158	\begin{proposition}[Radius-explicit path moments]
   159	  \label{P:radius-actual-moments}
   160	  Under~\eqref{E:radius-anchor-parameters}--\eqref{E:radius-anchor-Q}, for every
   161	  finite $v \ge 1$,
   162	  \begin{equation}\label{E:radius-actual-path-moments}
   163	    \|M_R(W)\|_{L^v(C^\theta([0,B];\mathcal{L}(E)))}
   164	    \le C_{Q,B}\sqrt v\,R^{d/Q},\qquad R\ge1.
   165	  \end{equation}
   166	  The constant does not depend on $v$ or $R$. This is an $E$ operator-path
   167	  estimate; the two constant columns on $F$ require their own estimates. Any
   168	  later projection used in a Cameron comparison must also satisfy its
   169	  orthogonality and covariance hypotheses.
   170	\end{proposition}
   171	
   172	\begin{proof}
   173	  Use the given smooth-test basis from Lemma~\ref{L:driver-noise-basis}, $g_j =
   174	  W(f_j)$, and its finite paths $M_N = \sum_{j\le N}g_jA_j$. These coefficient
   175	  paths use the same given noise as in Lemma~\ref{L:driver-holder-limit}, not
   176	  source approximations. Choose
   177	  \[
   178	    \rho=2R+B+2\le(B+4)R,\qquad \chi=\chi_0(\cdot/\rho).
   179	  \]
   180	  The plateau covers $B_{2R+B+1}$. Thus, both explicit localization identities
   181	  \eqref{E:driver-actual-localization} hold for this envelope. The physical
   182	  noise mask remains $m_R$. Both envelopes $K_{\rm in},K_{\rm out}$ here use
   183	  this same $\chi_\rho$.
   184	
   185	  For an interval $I \subset [0,B]$ of length $0 < h \le 1$,
   186	  Proposition~\ref{P:wave-two-variances} and
   187	  Lemma~\ref{L:driver-actual-variances} give both finite weighted variances with
   188	  bound $V_{B,\mathrm{var}}h^{2-a}B_\alpha(h)$, uniformly in $R,N,I$. In
   189	  particular, the base mask is the same fixed $\eta^2$ required by that variance
   190	  theorem. Corollary~\ref{C:finite-gaussian-operators}, applied in the balanced
   191	  coordinates, gives for every even $q \ge Q$
   192	  \[
   193	    \|M_N(I)\|_{L^q(S_q)}
   194	    \le\sqrt{q-1}\sqrt{V_{B,\mathrm{var}}}\,
   195	    h^{1-a/2}B_\alpha(h)^{1/2}\|K_{\rm out}\|_{S_q},
   196	  \]
   197	  where $B_\alpha(h)$ is $1$, $1+\log(1/h)$ or $h^{1-\alpha}$ according as
   198	  $\alpha < 1$, $\alpha = 1$ or $\alpha > 1$. Both variances and both
   199	  localizations have been checked; individual basis-dependent coefficient bounds
   200	  are not summed.
   201	
   202	  For $q \ge Q$, the unnormalized Schatten norms obey $\|K_{\rm out}\|_{S_q} \le
   203	  \|K_{\rm out}\|_{S_Q}$. Indeed, normalize a nonzero singular-value sequence by
   204	  its $\ell^Q$ norm; each entry is at most one, so its $q$th power sum is at
   205	  most its $Q$th power sum. The zero case is immediate.
   206	  Apply~\eqref{E:radius-two-envelopes} only at the fixed index $Q$. Use $\|A\|
   207	  \le \|A\|_{S_q}$ and $\sqrt{q-1} \le \sqrt q$. The balanced Hilbert
   208	  complexification has the same operator norm as its real restriction, and
   209	  $\rho^{d/Q} \le (B+4)^{d/Q}R^{d/Q}$. Since $\beta_t$ is strictly below the
   210	  corresponding short-time power, it follows that
   211	  \begin{equation}\label{E:radius-finite-increment}
   212	    \|M_N(t)-M_N(u)\|_{L^q(\mathcal{L}(E))}
   213	    \le C_{Q,B}\sqrt q\,R^{d/Q}|t-u|^{\beta_t},
   214	    \qquad |t-u|\le1.
   215	  \end{equation}
   216	  At $\alpha = 1$, the factor $\sqrt{1+\log(1/h)}$ is absorbed by the strict gap
   217	  $1-a/2-\beta_t > 0$. For $\alpha > 1$, the power is $(3-a-\alpha)/2$. These
   218	  power/log constants are independent of $R,N,q$. Longer increments are finite
   219	  sums of increments of length at most one, with constants depending only on the
   220	  fixed $B$.
   221	
   222	  Let $D_n(F)$ be the largest adjacent increment on the grid $kB2^{-n}$ of
   223	  $[0,B]$. For fine levels $B2^{-n} \le 1$, the finite-maximum bound gives
   224	  \[
   225	    \|D_n(M_N)\|_{L^q}
   226	    \le2^{n/q}C_{Q,B}\sqrt q\,R^{d/Q}(B2^{-n})^{\beta_t}.
   227	  \]
   228	  No independence of increments is used. The sum after multiplication by
   229	  $2^{n\eta_t}$ converges uniformly for even $q \ge Q$, because its geometric
   230	  ratio is at most $2^{-(\beta_t-\eta_t-1/Q)} < 1$. The finitely many coarse
   231	  levels are controlled by unit partitions. The deterministic dyadic chaining
   232	  argument in Lemma~\ref{L:driver-holder-limit} therefore bounds the
   233	  $L^qC^{\eta_t}$ norms by $C_{Q,B}\sqrt q\,R^{d/Q}$. Each finite path is
   234	  continuous and starts at zero, as required there. The fixed-horizon embedding
   235	  $C^{\eta_t}\hookrightarrow C^\theta$ gives the same estimate in $C^\theta$.
   236	
   237	  For each fixed $R$, Lemma~\ref{L:driver-holder-limit} identifies $M_R(W)$ as
   238	  the all-finite-moment $C^\theta$ limit of these very $M_N$. Pass the uniform
   239	  finite-$N$ estimate to this limit. Uniform convergence in $R$ is unnecessary:
   240	  the limiting bound has its explicit radius dependence at every $R$. For
   241	  arbitrary $v \ge 1$, choose an even $q \ge \max(v,Q)$ with $q \le v+Q+2 \le
   242	  (Q+3)v$. Lyapunov's inequality gives~\eqref{E:radius-actual-path-moments},
   243	  absorbing $\sqrt{Q+3}$ into the fixed constant. This proves
   244	  Proposition~\ref{P:radius-actual-moments}.
   245	\end{proof}

   278	\subsection{The growing-radius expected-norm anchor}
   279	
   280	\begin{proposition}[Averaged block mean tends to zero]
   281	  \label{P:radius-mean-anchor}
   282	  Fix integer $B \ge 1$ and use the true block partition $B,\delta,N,\ell_m$ of
   283	  Section~\ref{S:actual-cameron-mean}, with $0 < \delta < \min(1,1/B)$ and $N =
   284	  \lfloor1/(\delta B)\rfloor$. For $Y_m$ as in
   285	  Corollary~\ref{C:radius-covariance-residuals}, put
   286	  \[
   287	    X_m(u)=g_\delta M_R(Y_m)(\min(u,\ell_m)),\qquad
   288	    Z_\delta=\left(\delta\sum_{m=0}^N
   289	    \|X_m\|_{C^\theta}^p\right)^{1/p},\qquad
   290	    g_\delta=\delta^{(1-a)/2},
   291	  \]
   292	  for any fixed $p \ge 1$. Then
   293	  \begin{equation}\label{E:radius-mean-anchor}
   294	    \E Z_\delta\le(2/B)^{1/p}C_{Q,B}\sqrt p\,
   295	    g_\delta R^{d/Q}.
   296	  \end{equation}
   297	  In particular, for $R_\delta = \delta^{-1}+2$,
   298	  \begin{equation}\label{E:radius-mean-anchor-decay}
   299	    2\E Z_\delta
   300	    \le2(2/B)^{1/p}C_{Q,B}\sqrt p\,3^{d/Q}
   301	    \delta^{e_{\rm anchor}}\longrightarrow0,\qquad
   302	    e_{\rm anchor}=\frac{1-a}{2}-\frac dQ>0 .
   303	  \end{equation}
   304	  Both bounds are uniform in the deterministic orthogonal projection.
   305	\end{proposition}
   306	
   307	\begin{proof}
   308	  Stopping an interaction primitive starting at zero and extending it constantly
   309	  to $B$ does not increase its supremum or H\"older seminorm. An empty last
   310	  interval gives the zero path. Probability normalization and Lyapunov give
   311	  \begin{align*}
   312	    \E Z_\delta
   313	    &\le(\E Z_\delta^p)^{1/p}
   314	    =\left(\delta\sum_{m=0}^N
   315	    \E\|X_m\|_{C^\theta}^p\right)^{1/p}\\
   316	    &\le[\delta(N+1)]^{1/p}g_\delta
   317	    C_{Q,B}\sqrt p\,R^{d/Q}.
   318	  \end{align*}
   319	  This is linearity for a finite sum; no time-block independence or maximum over
   320	  blocks is used. Since $\delta B < 1$, we have $N \ge 1$ and $N+1 \le 2/(\delta
   321	  B)$, proving~\eqref{E:radius-mean-anchor}.
   322	
   323	  Now $R_\delta \le 3/\delta$ because $\delta < 1$. The last condition
   324	  in~\eqref{E:radius-anchor-Q} is equivalent to $Q(1-a) > 2d$. Dividing by $2Q >
   325	  0$ gives $e_{\rm anchor} > 0$. Substitute this radius
   326	  into~\eqref{E:radius-mean-anchor} to
   327	  obtain~\eqref{E:radius-mean-anchor-decay}. The estimate holds at each fixed
   328	  $B,p,Q$ and model, uniformly in every deterministic residual projection. This
   329	  proves Proposition~\ref{P:radius-mean-anchor}.
   330	\end{proof}
   331	
   332	These bounds concern the expected operator-path norm on $E$. They do not give an
   333	$F$ estimate with constant initial-data columns. The radius substitution is
   334	numerical; cone coverage and source-to-point transfer require their separate
   335	arguments. No concentration, integration over an infinite sequence of Gaussian

    51	\begin{lemma}[Coupled Gaussian block inputs]\label{L:raw-block-inputs}
    52	  Each $T_{\delta,m}$ is an isometry of the original test completion, respecting
    53	  covariance-null tests. All $W_{\delta,m}$ and $Z$ are on the same given noise
    54	  space, without an independence assertion. Let $\mathcal{K}(F)$ have the
    55	  operator norm and let $\mathscr{B}_0 = h_0^\theta([0,B];\mathcal{K}(F))$ be
    56	  the $C^\theta$ closure of zero-initial polygonal compact-operator paths. It is
    57	  a separable Banach space. In $\mathscr{B}_\delta = \mathscr{B}_0^{N+1}$ with
    58	  maximum norm, $(X,Z)$, $X = (X_m)_{m=0}^N$, is jointly centered Gaussian and
    59	  \begin{equation}\label{E:raw-block-covariance}
    60	    b:=\E[XZ]=\sqrt\delta\,H,\qquad H=(H_m)_{m=0}^N.
    61	  \end{equation}
    62	  Moreover,
    63	  \begin{equation}\label{E:raw-block-moments}
    64	    \|X_m\|_{L^p\mathscr{B}_0}
    65	    \le C_{R,B}\sqrt p\,g_\delta,\qquad p\ge1.
    66	  \end{equation}
    67	\end{lemma}
    68	
    69	\begin{proof}
    70	  Substituting $s = s_m+\delta u$, $t = s_m+\delta r$ in the original covariance
    71	  gives the factor $\delta^{a-2}\delta^2\delta^{-a} = 1$. Thus, the maps extend
    72	  isometrically through the null quotient. Direct test substitution gives
    73	  $W_{\delta,m}(f) = W_{\mathrm{fast}}(f(\cdot-mB,\cdot))$. These are explicit
    74	  common-space identities.
    75	
    76	  Finite-rank rational matrices in a countable real Hilbert basis are dense in
    77	  $\mathcal{K}(F)$: for compact $T$, $P_nTP_n \to T$ in norm by compactness of
    78	  $T,T^*$, and finite entries admit rational approximation. Polygonal paths with
    79	  rational breakpoints and such matrices give separability of $\mathscr{B}_0$.
    80	  To approximate breakpoints, use uniform convergence, uniform Lipschitz bounds
    81	  and $[f]_\theta \le (2\|f\|_\infty)^{1-\theta}\operatorname{Lip}(f)^\theta$.
    82	  The same inequality puts every zero-initial Lipschitz compact-valued path in
    83	  $\mathscr{B}_0$ by polygonal approximation. The finite original coefficient
    84	  paths $iA_jL_\psi$ have these properties. Their Gaussian sums converge in
    85	  $L^pC^\theta$ and hence in the closed space $\mathscr{B}_0$. Their laws and
    86	  the parent Gaussian norm bound give~\eqref{E:raw-block-moments}. Every finite
    87	  joint coefficient list with $Z$ is Gaussian on the same $W$. Scalar continuous
    88	  functionals pass through the $L^2$ limits, preserving Gaussianity by
    89	  convergence of variances and characteristic functions. Thus, $(X,Z)$ is the
    90	  asserted Banach Gaussian variable. Cauchy--Schwarz gives $\E\|XZ\| \le
    91	  \|X\|_2\sqrt v < \infty$, so its Bochner covariance exists.
    92	
    93	  The original covariance and the test pullback give
    94	  \begin{equation}\label{E:raw-block-mean-jacobian}
    95	    \E[W_{\delta,m}(f)Z]
    96	    =\delta^{a/2}\int f(u,x)h_{s_m+\delta u}(x)\ud x\ud u.
    97	  \end{equation}
    98	  Absolute Fubini uses compact supports, local Radon mass and $a < 1$. This
    99	  identity extends to the explicit matrix-element tests for the operator path on
   100	  $E$: their time indicator is approximated by smooth bounded tests on one
   101	  compact support, converging in the original covariance norm by dominated
   102	  convergence against $|u-r|^{-a}\Gamma$; their mean pairings converge as well.
   103	  The Sobolev adjoint is the one in~\eqref{E:driver-covariance-row}. Hence, the
   104	  path covariance is $g_\delta\delta^{a/2}H_m = \sqrt\delta\,H_m$ on real
   105	  Schwartz $E$ pairs. For constant inputs the two columns are the same $L_\psi$
   106	  inputs $(\psi,0)$ and $(0,\psi)$, and total finite propagation identifies
   107	  their deterministic response. The span of $E$ and both constant coordinates is
   108	  dense in $F$; $E$ alone is not. Boundedness, rational times and path
   109	  continuity prove~\eqref{E:raw-block-covariance} on all $F$. In particular, $H
   110	  = b/\sqrt\delta \in \mathscr{B}_\delta$. This proves
   111	  Lemma~\ref{L:raw-block-inputs}.
   112	\end{proof}

   114	\begin{proposition}[Change of law on the whole norm-Borel space]
   115	  \label{P:raw-block-gaussian-law}
   116	  For every nonnegative norm-Borel $j$ on all of $\mathscr{B}_\delta$,
   117	  \begin{equation}\label{E:raw-block-gaussian-law}
   118	    \E j(X)=
   119	    \E\left[e^{-Z/\sqrt\delta-v/(2\delta)}j(X+H)\right].
   120	  \end{equation}
   121	  The equality is valid also as an extended nonnegative integral.
   122	\end{proposition}
   123	
   124	\begin{proof}
   125	  For real $s$, the density $e^{-sZ-s^2v/2}$ defines an equivalent probability
   126	  measure $Q_s$ by completing the square in the $N(0,v)$ density. For any finite
   127	  list $\ell$ of continuous real coordinates on $\mathscr{B}_\delta$, the
   128	  Gaussian vector $(\ell(X),Z)$ is equal in law to $(TG,z\cdot G)$ for a finite
   129	  standard Gaussian vector $G$. A positive covariance square root gives this
   130	  representation even when singular; no inverse is used. Here $Tz = \ell(b)$ and
   131	  $|z|^2 = v$. Substitution $G' = G+sz$ in its density gives
   132	  $\E_{Q_s}f(\ell(X+sb)) = \E f(\ell(X))$ for every bounded Borel $f$.
   133	
   134	  The matrix entries of each block in a real Hilbert basis at rational times,
   135	  together with $0,B$, generate the norm-Borel sigma-field. To see the
   136	  operator-norm point, for a countable dense set $\mathcal{D}$ of unit vectors
   137	  obtained from normalized rational finite basis combinations, $\|T\| =
   138	  \sup_{u,w\in\mathcal{D}}|\langle Tu,w\rangle|$. These pairings are finite
   139	  linear combinations of matrix entries. Supremum and H\"older norms of
   140	  continuous paths are suprema over rational times and pairs. Thus, distance to
   141	  every fixed element of $\mathscr{B}_\delta$ is coordinate-measurable. Open
   142	  balls are measurable by rational closed-ball approximation, and separability
   143	  makes every open set a countable union of balls from dense centers. Conversely
   144	  the coordinates are continuous. The cylinder sets form a generating pi-system;
   145	  uniqueness of probability measures extends the finite-coordinate equality to
   146	  all norm-Borel sets. Simple functions and monotone convergence give the
   147	  identity for nonnegative $j$. Finally, take $s = \delta^{-1/2}$ and use $sb =
   148	  H$ from~\eqref{E:raw-block-covariance}. The map and its deterministic
   149	  translate are defined on the entire input space; there is no translated
   150	  exceptional-domain assumption. This proves
   151	  Proposition~\ref{P:raw-block-gaussian-law}.
   152	\end{proof}

   156	For any $x \in \mathscr{B}_0$ define $D_x(u) = S_F(u)U_x(u,0)$ by the

   161	\begin{lemma}[Uniform block error]\label{L:raw-block-uniform-error}
   162	  Let $M_\delta = \max_{m\le N}\|X_m\|_{\mathscr{B}_0}$, including its factor
   163	  $g_\delta$. Then $M_\delta \to 0$ in every finite $L^q$, and, for some $c >
   164	  0$,
   165	  \begin{equation}\label{E:raw-block-maximum-exponential}
   166	    \sup_\delta\E e^{cM_\delta^2}<\infty.
   167	  \end{equation}
   168	  With the deterministic $P_s$ in~\eqref{E:compact-F-block},
   169	  \begin{equation}\label{E:raw-block-operator-error}
   170	    E_{\mathrm{op},\delta}:=
   171	    \max_{m\le N}\sup_{0\le u\le B}
   172	    \|D_m^+(u)-P_{s_m}(u)\|_{\mathcal{B}(F)}
   173	    \longrightarrow0
   174	    \quad\hbox{in every finite }L^q.
   175	  \end{equation}
   176	\end{lemma}
   177	
   178	\begin{proof}
   179	  The maximum and~\eqref{E:raw-block-moments}, with $N+1 \le 2/\delta$, give
   180	  \[
   181	    \|M_\delta\|_p
   182	    \le (N+1)^{1/p}C\sqrt p\,g_\delta
   183	    \le C'\sqrt p\,\delta^{(1-a)/2-1/p}.
   184	  \]
   185	  For fixed $q$, choose $p > \max(q,2/(1-a))$ to prove the first limit. No
   186	  independence is needed. Choose an integer $n_0$ with $n_0(1-a) \ge 1$. For $n
   187	  \ge n_0$,
   188	  \[
   189	    \E M_\delta^{2n}
   190	    \le2C^{2n}(2n)^n\delta^{n(1-a)-1}
   191	    \le2C^{2n}(2n)^n.
   192	  \]
   193	  For $1 \le n < n_0$, Lyapunov bounds the moment by the appropriate power of
   194	  the $2n_0$ moment. These finitely many terms are bounded. For the remaining
   195	  exponential series, $n! \ge (n/e)^n$ gives a geometric tail $2\sum_{n\ge
   196	  n_0}(2ecC^2)^n$ for small $c$. This
   197	  proves~\eqref{E:raw-block-maximum-exponential}; no such assertion is made for
   198	  the unscaled maximum.
   199	
   200	  Let $H_m^{\mathrm{stat}}$ be the primitive for constant potential $V_{s_m}$.
   201	  Compact mea smoothness on $[0,2]$ and the statewise primitive bound give
   202	  \[
   203	    \sup_m\max(\|H_m\|_{C^\theta},
   204	    \|H_m^{\mathrm{stat}}\|_{C^\theta})\le H_0,\qquad
   205	    \sup_m\|H_m-H_m^{\mathrm{stat}}\|_{C^\theta}\le C\delta.
   206	  \]
   207	  Indeed, the potential difference is at most $C\delta B$ in $L^\infty$ and
   208	  $L^2$; integration of the bounded free groups gives its Lipschitz primitive
   209	  bound on this fixed horizon. On $\{M_\delta\le1\}$, local Young stability on
   210	  the fixed ball of radius $H_0+1$ gives $E_{\mathrm{op},\delta} \le
   211	  C(M_\delta+\delta)$. This proves convergence in probability. The global Young
   212	  bound also gives
   213	  \[
   214	    \max_m\sup_{u\le B}\|D_m^+(u)\|
   215	    \le C_B\exp\big(C_B(1+H_0+M_\delta)^{1/\theta}\big).
   216	  \]
   217	  Since $1/\theta < 2$, every finite power of this bound is dominated by a
   218	  constant times the exponential in~\eqref{E:raw-block-maximum-exponential}.
   219	  Uniform higher moments yield uniform integrability, proving
   220	  \eqref{E:raw-block-operator-error}. Suprema are measurable: on a countable
   221	  dense set of unit states each difference is continuous in $u$, so rational
   222	  times and those states suffice. Operator-norm continuity of the physical free
   223	  group is not used. Only $s_m \le 1$ supplies the ground templates. This proves
   224	  Lemma~\ref{L:raw-block-uniform-error}.
   225	\end{proof}

   227	\begin{lemma}[Indexed cone and terminal displacement]
   228	  \label{L:raw-block-indexed-cone}
   229	  Fix $0 < \varrho < 1/2$. There are an integer $B \ge 1$ and positive
   230	  $\omega,\epsilon_{\mathrm{op}},c_*$ such that the following holds for every $N

231	  \ge 1$. If $\sigma_0,\ldots,\sigma_N \in I$ have adjacent distances at most
   232	  $\omega$ and real bounded operator families $D_m(u)$, $0 \le u \le B$, satisfy
   233	  \[
   234	    \max_{m\le N}\sup_{0\le u\le B}
   235	    \|D_m(u)-P_{\sigma_m}(u)\|\le\epsilon_{\mathrm{op}},
   236	  \]
   237	  then, for $0 \le u \le B$,
   238	  \begin{equation}\label{E:raw-block-positive-product}
   239	    O_\phi D_N(u)D_{N-1}(B)\cdots D_0(B)e_0
   240	    \ge c_*(1-\varrho)^{N-1}
   241	    \exp\left(B\sum_{m<N}\lambda_{\sigma_m}
   242	    +u\lambda_{\sigma_N}\right)>0.
   243	  \end{equation}
   244	  No positivity, composition or independence assumption on the $D_m$ is
   245	  required.
   246	\end{lemma}
   247	
   248	\begin{proof}
   249	  From~\eqref{E:compact-normalized-complement} fix $C_{\mathrm{gap}} \ge 1$,
   250	  $\eta_{\mathrm{gap}} > 0$ so the normalized complementary norm is at most
   251	  $C_{\mathrm{gap}}e^{-\eta_{\mathrm{gap}}t}$. Define positive margins and
   252	  finite bounds
   253	  \[
   254	    a_*=\inf_I\ell_s(e_0),\quad j_*=\inf_I O_\phi(e_s),\quad
   255	    M_e=\max(1,\sup_I\|e_s\|),\quad
   256	    M_\ell=\max(1,\sup_I\|\ell_s\|).
   257	  \]
   258	  Also put $M_P = \max(1,\sup_I\|\Pi_s\|)$, $M_Q = 1+M_P$, $M_z = M_e+1$, $E_0 =
   259	  \|e_0\| = 1$ and $H_{\mathrm{obs}} = \max(1,\|O_\phi\|)$. Choose the aperture
   260	  \emph{first}: $\vartheta = \min(1,j_*/(16H_{\mathrm{obs}}C_{\mathrm{gap}})) >
   261	  0$. Next choose integer $B \ge 1$ with
   262	  \[
   263	    q_B:=C_{\mathrm{gap}}e^{-\eta_{\mathrm{gap}}B}
   264	    \le\min\left(\frac18,\frac{\vartheta a_*}{8M_QE_0}\right).
   265	  \]
   266	  Choose $\nu > 0$ such that $\nu M_z \le \min(\varrho/2,\vartheta,1/4)$.
   267	  Uniform continuity of $\ell_s,\Pi_s$ supplies $\omega > 0$ for which adjacent
   268	  distances at most $\omega$ give both norm differences at most $\nu$. Finally,
   269	  choose $\epsilon_{\mathrm{op}} > 0$ satisfying all five smallness conditions
   270	  \begin{align*}
   271	    M_\ell\epsilon_{\mathrm{op}}M_z&\le\varrho/2,&
   272	    M_Q\epsilon_{\mathrm{op}}M_z&\le\vartheta/4,\\
   273	    M_\ell\epsilon_{\mathrm{op}}E_0&\le a_*/2,&
   274	    M_Q\epsilon_{\mathrm{op}}E_0&\le\vartheta a_*/8,&
   275	    H_{\mathrm{obs}}\epsilon_{\mathrm{op}}M_z&\le j_*/8.
   276	  \end{align*}
   277	  All denominators are positive. This order of choices uses the normalized
   278	  complement rather than a growing terminal norm.
   279	
   280	  The cone at $s$ consists of $z = Ae_s+r$, with $A = \ell_s(z) > 0$, $\ell_s(r)
   281	  = 0$ and $\|r\|_F \le \vartheta A$. In particular, $r = Q_sz$ and $\|z\| \le
   282	  M_zA$. For entrance, $z_1 = D_0(B)e_0$, with $b = \sigma_0$, has normalized
   283	  amplitude at least $a_*-M_\ell\epsilon_{\mathrm{op}}E_0 \ge a_*/2$. Its
   284	  normalized residual is at most $q_BM_QE_0+M_Q\epsilon_{\mathrm{op}}E_0 \le
   285	  \vartheta a_*/4$. Thus, it enters the cone with residual ratio at most
   286	  $\vartheta/2$ and amplitude at least $e^{\lambda_bB}a_*/2$.
   287	
   288	  For an old-cone state $z = Ae_b+r$ and an adjacent index $c$, rebase before
   289	  using the complementary estimate:
   290	  \[
   291	    \ell_c(z)\ge(1-\nu M_z)A,\qquad
   292	    \|Q_cz\|\le\|Q_bz\|+\|(\Pi_b-\Pi_c)z\|
   293	    \le(\vartheta+\nu M_z)A.
   294	  \]

   296	  e^{-\lambda_cB}\ell_c(Dz)$ and $y = e^{-\lambda_cB}\|Q_cDz\|$. Since
   297	  $\lambda_c > 0$, the perturbation and smallness conditions give
   298	  \[
   299	    x\ge(1-\nu M_z-M_\ell\epsilon_{\mathrm{op}}M_z)A
   300	    \ge(1-\varrho)A>A/2,
   301	  \]
   302	  and
   303	  \[
   304	    y\le
   305	    [q_B(\vartheta+\nu M_z)+M_Q\epsilon_{\mathrm{op}}M_z]A
   306	    \le\vartheta A/2.
   307	  \]

   309	  $M_Q\epsilon_{\mathrm{op}}M_z \le \vartheta/4$. Together with $\varrho < 1/2$,
   310	  these give $y \le \vartheta x$. These are precisely the finite residual and
   311	  cone-conversion margins; the old residual was not assumed to lie in the new
   312	  kernel. Each full block therefore preserves the new cone and multiplies its
   313	  amplitude by at least $e^{\lambda_cB}(1-\varrho)$.

   315	  For the terminal $0 \le u \le B$, rebase once more to $c = \sigma_N$. The same
   316	  bounds give $\ell_c(z) \ge 3A/4$ and $\|Q_cz\| \le 2\vartheta A$.

   323	  $H_{\mathrm{obs}}\epsilon_{\mathrm{op}}M_z \le j_*/8$. Since
   324	  $16H_{\mathrm{obs}}C_{\mathrm{gap}}\vartheta \le j_*$, the result is at least

   327	  a_*j_*/4$. The induction is empty for $N = 1$ and the estimate includes $u =

   333	\begin{lemma}[Composition over time blocks and regularized products]
   334	  \label{L:raw-block-restart}
   335	  Fix $\delta,B,N$ and let $L = \delta^{-1}$, $L_{\mathrm{ext}} = (N+1)B \ge L$.
   336	  On this global fast horizon define $A_{\mathrm{glob}} = g_\delta
   337	  A_R(W_{\mathrm{fast}})$. Its physical flow obeys
   338	  \begin{equation}\label{E:raw-block-restart}
   339	    P_{\mathrm{glob}}(mB+u,mB)=D_m^0(u),\qquad 0\le u\le B.
   340	  \end{equation}
   341	  The analogous identity holds with the deterministic mean $V_{\delta t}$ added
   342	  globally and local operator paths $X_m+H_m$. Their finite block products,
   343	  including the last remainder $\tau$, are source limits in $L^2$, at this fixed
   344	  $\delta,N$.
   345	\end{lemma}
   346	
   347	\begin{proof}
   348	  Take one regularized slow noise preserving the given noise $Y_{\epsilon,\eta}$
   349	  on the extension of the given $W$ constructed in
   350	  Section~\ref{S:source-driver-convergence}. Define the fast and local noises by
   351	  \[
   352	    Y_{\mathrm{fast}}(f)=Y_{\epsilon,\eta}(T_{\delta,0}f),\qquad
   353	    Y_m(f)=Y_{\epsilon,\eta}(T_{\delta,m}f).
   354	  \]
   355	  The pullback isometry and~\eqref{E:source-two-dominations} give source and
   356	  residual variance bounds by $\|f\|_{H_W}^2$. The residual tends to zero on
   357	  each transformed smooth compact test at fixed $\delta,m$. Joint Gaussianity is
   358	  retained. Proposition~\ref{P:source-gaussian-transfer} therefore gives the
   359	  $L^pC^\theta$ operator-path limits on $[0,L_{\mathrm{ext}}]$ and on $[0,B]$,
   360	  including both constant columns.
   361	
   362	  Their random fields are $Y_{\mathrm{fast}}(u,x) =
   363	  \delta^{a/2}Y_{\epsilon,\eta}(\delta u,x)$ and $Y_m(u,x) =
   364	  Y_{\mathrm{fast}}(mB+u,x)$. Indeed, these follow by change of variables in
   365	  their test integrals. The temporal law is $K_{\eta/\delta}$ because
   366	  $\delta^aK_\eta(\delta r) = K_{\eta/\delta}(r)$; the spatial heat law and all
   367	  joint width rules are unchanged. They are continuous in time and smooth in
   368	  space. Their ordinary primitives equal their Gaussian operator paths: their
   369	  matrix entries are $Y_m(h_R)$, by the indicator approximation used
   370	  in~\eqref{E:raw-block-mean-jacobian} and the point-test integral identity.
   371	  Total finite propagation extends this identity to both constant columns. This
   372	  does not assume a separately chosen extension preserving the given noise
   373	  automatically commutes with time dilation.
   374	
   375	  Changing the ordinary source integration variable and composing the free
   376	  groups gives the exact identity on $F$
   377	  \[

   104	  Translations $\tau_y$ on both entries are isometries on $E$ and commute with
   105	  $S_E(h)$. For fixed $z,w \in E$, their translated pairing is the Fourier
   106	  transform of an $L^1$ function: the two weighted Fourier products are
   107	  integrable by Cauchy--Schwarz in the Bessel norms. Approximation of that
   108	  function in $L^1$ by compact smooth functions, followed by integration by
   109	  parts for the approximants, proves $\langle\tau_yz,w\rangle_E \to 0$ as $|y|
   110	  \to \infty$. Thus, $\tau_yz$ tends weakly to zero. For compact $K$,
   111	  $\|K\tau_yz\| \to 0$: otherwise compactness supplies a norm-convergent
   112	  subsequence with nonzero norm, while bounded linear testing makes its limit
   113	  zero. For unit $z$ it follows that
   114	  \[
   115	    \|S_E(h)+K\|
   116	    \ge\liminf_{|y|\to\infty}\|(S_E(h)+K)\tau_yz\|
   117	    \ge\|S_E(h)z\|.
   118	  \]
   119	  Taking the supremum over $z$ gives $\|S_E(h)+K\| \ge \|S_E(h)\|$. The
   120	  isometric velocity reversal $\mathcal{R}(u,v) = (u,-v)$ satisfies $S_E(-h) =
   121	  \mathcal{R} S_E(h)\mathcal{R}$ by the full free Fourier matrix. The group law
   122	  yields $1 \le \|S_E(-h)\|\|S_E(h)\| = \|S_E(h)\|^2$. This
   123	  proves~\eqref{E:symplectic-compact-young-baseline}.
   124	
   125	  Finally, $P_j-S_E(\ell_j)$ is compact. Telescoping the finite ordered product
   126	  against its free product gives a finite sum of bounded--compact--bounded
   127	  products, hence a compact difference. Only the free factors are combined by
   128	  the group law; no noisy factors are commuted. The same translation argument
   129	  proves \eqref{E:symplectic-compact-product-baseline}. A zero length gives $P_j
   130	  = I$. All assertions are at fixed finite horizons and products; no uniform
   131	  compact approximation in a radius, horizon or number of factors is asserted.
   132	  This proves Lemma~\ref{L:symplectic-free}.
   133	\end{proof}

   135	\begin{lemma}[Covariance means and source primitives]
   136	  \label{L:symplectic-source-mean}
   137	  The expectations in~\eqref{E:symplectic-combined-driver} are Bochner defined
   138	  and
   139	  \begin{equation}\label{E:symplectic-mean-convergence}
   140	    \|D_\Phi^\rho-D_\Phi\|_{C^\theta}
   141	    \le\|\Phi\|_{H_W}\|M^\rho-M\|_{L^2C^\theta}\longrightarrow0 .
   142	  \end{equation}

   144	  spatially smooth $h_\Phi^\rho$ such that
   145	  \begin{equation}\label{E:symplectic-source-primitive}
   146	    D_\Phi^\rho(t)
   147	    =\int_0^t S_E(-r)B(m_Rh_\Phi^\rho(r))S_E(r)\ud r .
   148	  \end{equation}
   149	  This is the statewise primitive and defines a Lipschitz operator path. The
   150	  combined source coefficient is $b^\rho = m_R(cY^\rho+h_\Phi^\rho)$.
   151	\end{lemma}
   152	
   153	\begin{proof}
   154	  Separable Gaussian path moments give $\E\|ZM\|_{C^\theta} \le
   155	  \|\Phi\|_{H_W}\|M\|_{L^2C^\theta}$, and the same holds for sources. Bochner
   156	  Cauchy--Schwarz gives~\eqref{E:symplectic-mean-convergence}. Covariance
   157	  contraction also gives the uniform source bound $\|D_\Phi^\rho\|_{C^\theta}
   158	  \le \|\Phi\|_{H_W}\|M\|_{L^2C^\theta}$.
   159	
   160	  The construction preserving the given noise has an isometry $j_{\rm src}:H_W
   161	  \to \mathcal{G}$ and an isonormal process $\mathcal{I}$ with
   162	  $\mathcal{I}(j_{\rm src}h) = W(h)$. Its source random field is $Y^\rho(t,x) =
   163	  \mathcal{I}(v_{\rho;t,x})$, with continuous $\mathcal{G}$-valued spatial
   164	  derivatives at positive widths. Consequently,
   165	  \[
   166	    h_\Phi^\rho(t,x)=\E[W(\Phi)Y^\rho(t,x)]
   167	    =\langle j_{\rm src}\Phi,v_{\rho;t,x}\rangle_{\mathcal{G}}
   168	  \]
   169	  has the claimed regularity. Bounded linear testing commutes with those
   170	  derivatives. After multiplication by $m_R$ the coefficient has one compact
   171	  support and bounded derivatives on $[0,T]$.
   172	
   173	  On Schwartz states, the row of the right side
   174	  of~\eqref{E:symplectic-source-primitive} is the integral of $h_\Phi^\rho$
   175	  against the explicit masked source wave product. Ordinary Fubini is justified
   176	  by $\E|ZY^\rho(t,x)| \le \|\Phi\|_{H_W} \sqrt{\E|Y^\rho(t,x)|^2}$ and bounded
   177	  point variance on this fixed compact set at positive widths. The source test
   178	  and indicator approximation extends this to the completed rows by Gaussian
   179	  Cauchy--Schwarz and covariance contraction. Hence, this row is the row of
   180	  $\E[ZM^\rho(t)]$. Countable dense states and rational times, then continuity,
   181	  identify the operator path. The uniformly bounded integrand gives its
   182	  Lipschitz bound. This identifies the combined source coefficient exactly. The
   183	  combined source is generally noncentered and the mask occurs once. This proves
   184	  Lemma~\ref{L:symplectic-source-mean}.
   185	\end{proof}

   187	\begin{proposition}[Source conservation]\label{P:symplectic-source}
   188	  At each fixed positive $\rho$, on one probability-one set for the fixed
   189	  $c,\Phi,R,T$, the physical source flow satisfies
   190	  \[
   191	    P_{D^\rho}(t,s)^*J_EP_{D^\rho}(t,s)=J_E,
   192	    \qquad 0\le s\le t\le T .
   193	  \]
   194	\end{proposition}
   195	
   196	\begin{proof}
   197	  Intersect the source coefficient regularity event with the event identifying
   198	  its first primitive with the ordinary primitive for all times and states. The
   199	  source construction supplies both at this fixed $\rho$. On their intersection
   200	  $b^\rho$ has a common compact support, is continuous in supremum norm and is
   201	  uniformly bounded on $[0,T]$. Thus, $C_b(r) = S_E(-r)B(b^\rho(r))S_E(r)$ is
   202	  uniformly bounded and strongly continuous on states.
   203	  Lemma~\ref{L:symplectic-free} gives $\omega(C_b(r)z,w)+\omega(z,C_b(r)w) = 0$
   204	  for all $r,z,w$.
   205

206	  The source and mean primitive identities identify the Young state equation
   207	  with $U(t,s)e = e+\int_s^t C_b(r)U(r,s)e\ud r$. Indeed, replace each operator
   208	  path increment in a Young sum by its statewise integral. The error is bounded
   209	  by the uniform coefficient bound times the uniform continuity error of $U$ on
   210	  the partition. Each state trajectory is therefore $C^1$, with derivative
   211	  $C_b(t)U(t,s)e$, by the strong-integral difference quotient. Differentiating
   212	  the bounded bilinear form $\omega(U(t,s)e,U(t,s)f)$ gives zero. This holds on
   213	  the same path set for all states and time pairs, since the bounded ordinary
   214	  evolution is defined there on all $E$. Free conjugation gives the displayed
   215	  physical identity. No uncountable intersection of state-dependent null sets or
   216	  derivative of the free generator on a rough state was used. This proves
   217	  Proposition~\ref{P:symplectic-source}.
   218	\end{proof}

   220	\begin{proposition}[Conservation, inverse and a lower norm bound]
   221	  \label{P:symplectic-raw}
   222	  For the fixed parameters in~\eqref{E:symplectic-combined-driver}, on one
   223	  probability-one set,
   224	  \begin{equation}\label{E:symplectic-raw-conservation}
   225	    P_D(t,s)^*J_EP_D(t,s)=J_E,\qquad
   226	    \|P_D(t,s)\|\ge1,\qquad 0\le s\le t\le T .
   227	  \end{equation}
   228	  The flow is invertible. For $c = 0$ these assertions are deterministic for
   229	  every fixed $\Phi$.
   230	\end{proposition}
   231	
   232	\begin{proof}
   233	  We first identify a closed real linear constraint on the operator path. Write
   234	  \[
   235	    \mathfrak{g}_J=\{A\in\mathcal{L}(E):A^*J_E+J_EA=0\}.
   236	  \]
   237	  The coefficient $H_{j,R}$ in~\eqref{E:driver-covariance-coefficient} is real
   238	  and smooth. Free conservation gives $S_E(-r)^*J_E = J_ES_E(r)$ and $J_ES_E(-r)
   239	  = S_E(r)^*J_E$. Lemma~\ref{L:symplectic-free} therefore makes
   240	  $S_E(-r)B(H_{j,R}(r))S_E(r)$ belong to $\mathfrak{g}_J$. Testing the statewise
   241	  integral in~\eqref{E:driver-coefficient-operator} against two states shows
   242	  $A_j(0,t) \in \mathfrak{g}_J$ for every $j,t$. No operator-norm derivative of
   243	  the free group is taken. The real finite sums
   244	  in~\eqref{E:driver-path-convergence} obey the same constraint. The map
   245	  $A\mapsto A^*J_E+J_EA$ is bounded on the path space, so their $L^2C^\theta$
   246	  limit $M$ obeys it at all times on one probability-one path set.
   247	
   248	  The mean is a Bochner expectation since $\E\|W(\Phi)M\|_{C^\theta} \le
   249	  \|\Phi\|_{H_W}\|M\|_{L^2C^\theta} < \infty$. Bounded real linear maps commute
   250	  with this expectation, hence $D_\Phi(t) \in \mathfrak{g}_J$ for every $t$.
   251	  Thus, $D = cM+D_\Phi$ starts at zero and is a $C^\theta$ path in
   252	  $\mathfrak{g}_J$ on that path set. Complex Gaussian coefficients are not used.
   253	  All these variables remain on the given $W$.
   254	
   255	  The proof of Proposition~\ref{P:constant-young-linear} applies on
   256	  $\mathcal{L}(E)$, with multiplication of norm one. Fix any $s$ and put $V(r) =
   257	  U_D(r,s)$ for $r \ge s$. The Young remainder on $[u,v] \subset [s,T]$ gives
   258	  \[
   259	    V(v)-V(u)=D_{u,v}V(u)+R_{u,v},\qquad
   260	    \|R_{u,v}\|\le C|v-u|^{2\theta}.
   261	  \]
   262	  The exact increment of $V^*J_EV$ has first-order term
   263	  $V(u)^*(D_{u,v}^*J_E+J_ED_{u,v})V(u) = 0$. Its remaining terms have norm at
   264	  most $C'|v-u|^{2\theta}$, using the bounded $C^\theta$ norm of $V$. Their sum
   265	  on a partition is at most $C'(t-s)\operatorname{mesh}^{2\theta-1}$, which
   266	  tends to zero. Therefore, $U_D(t,s)^*J_EU_D(t,s) = J_E$. This deterministic
   267	  argument applies to every time pair on the same operator path; it requires no
   268	  state-dependent null sets. Free conservation in Lemma~\ref{L:symplectic-free}
   269	  gives \eqref{E:symplectic-raw-conservation}, including $1 = \|J_E\| \le
   270	  \|P_D(t,s)\|^2$.
   271	
   272	  Invertibility comes from the local Young Neumann pieces and their finite
   273	  products, followed by the free inverse; it is not inferred from conservation
   274	  in infinite dimension. For $c = 0$ the path and the argument are deterministic
   275	  for each $\Phi$. Zero covariance gives the free flow directly. At each fixed
   276	  $\delta$ one may take the given reference $W\circ T_{\delta,0}$, $R =
   277	  \delta^{-1}+2$, $T = \delta^{-1}$, $c = g_\delta$ and $\Phi = 0$. No
   278	  uniform-radius or uniform bound for controls assertion follows. This proves
   279	  Proposition~\ref{P:symplectic-raw}.
   280	\end{proof}

   282	\begin{proposition}[The exact completed block mean]\label{P:symplectic-block-mean}
   283	  Use the true partition $B,\delta,N,s_m,\ell_m$ of
   284	  Section~\ref{S:actual-cameron-mean}, with integer $B \ge 1$. Let $i_I:H_I \to
   285	  H_W$ be the supported closed inclusion and $T_m = T_{\delta,m}:H_{\rm fast}
   286	  \to H_W$ the original isometry; $H_{\rm fast}$ has the same original
   287	  covariance in fast coordinates. For $\Phi \in H_I$ set
   288	  \[
   289	    W_m(f)=W(T_mf),\qquad
   290	    \phi_m=\delta^{-a/2}T_m^*i_I\Phi,\qquad
   291	    \mathcal{T}_E\Phi=i^*T\Phi\,i ,
   292	  \]
   293	  where $T$ is the full $F$ mean of Proposition~\ref{P:cameron-full-mean}.
   294	  Define
   295	  \begin{equation}\label{E:symplectic-block-primitive}
   296	    H_{m,E}(\Phi)(u)=\int_0^{\min(u,\ell_m)}
   297	    S_E(-v)\mathcal{T}_E\Phi(s_m+\delta v)S_E(v)\ud v .
   298	  \end{equation}
   299	  With $M_m = M_R(W_m)$ and $D_{\phi_m}(u) = \E[M_m(u)W_m(\phi_m)]$, one has
   300	  \begin{equation}\label{E:symplectic-block-direction}
   301	    D_{\phi_m}(\min(u,\ell_m))=H_{m,E}(\Phi)(u),\qquad 0\le u\le B .
   302	  \end{equation}
   303	  Consequently, the pure-mean endpoint obeys
   304	  \[
   305	    \|S_E(\ell_m)U_{H_{m,E}(\Phi)}(\ell_m,0)\|\ge1 .
   306	  \]
   307	\end{proposition}
   308	
   309	\begin{proof}
   310	  The original pullback~\eqref{E:raw-block-pullback} has covariance factor
   311	  $\delta^{a-2}\delta^2\delta^{-a} = 1$, hence respects nulls and extends
   312	  isometrically from fast to slow original space. Its Hilbert adjoint is a
   313	  contraction. Thus, $\|\phi_m\| \le \delta^{-a/2}\|\Phi\|$ is finite at fixed
   314	  $\delta$, without a uniform control-radius assertion. The fast noise remains
   315	  on the same given $W$. For applying the preceding propositions, construct
   316	  regularized noises with $W_m$ as the given reference, extending by an
   317	  independent auxiliary source while retaining all base variables. No
   318	  slow-source pullback is presumed; the original covariance direction is
   319	  independent of the auxiliary realization.
   320	
   321	  The mean $T\Phi$ has range in closed $iE$. By
   322	  Proposition~\ref{P:cameron-full-mean}, bounded compression passes its strong
   323	  measurability, $L^r$ bound and compact operator values to $\mathcal{T}_E\Phi
   324	  \in L^r(I;\mathcal{K}(E))$. Choose the full parameter
   325	  choices~\eqref{E:cameron-block-parameters}. Its intervals are nonempty because
   326	  $\theta < 1-a/2$ and $\theta > 1/2$; $p$ only instantiates that package here.
   327	  The compact-conjugation argument makes \eqref{E:symplectic-block-primitive} a
   328	  Bochner integral, and the $L^r$ primitive estimate gives $C^\theta$, since
   329	  $1-1/r > \theta$. Affine pullback preserves null sets. Its integrand is
   330	  compact valued almost everywhere; closedness of $\mathcal{K}(E)$ under Bochner
   331	  integration makes $H_{m,E}(\Phi)$ a compact-valued path starting at zero, also
   332	  after constant stopping.
   333	
   334	  Here $A_{F,m}$ is the full $F$ interaction operator path from
   335	  Proposition~\ref{P:constant-phase-driver}, and $H_{m,F}$ is its stopped
   336	  completed mean primitive in~\eqref{E:cameron-actual-covariance}. The completed
   337	  identity~\eqref{E:cameron-actual-covariance} at original projection rank zero
   338	  gives, for $0 \le u \le \ell_m$,
   339	  \[
   340	    \E[g_\delta A_{F,m}(u)W(i_I\Phi)]
   341	    =\sqrt\delta\,H_{m,F}(\Phi)(u).
   342	  \]
   343	  Compress through $i$ using the operator path intertwining, $S_Fi = iS_E$, and
   344	  the mean range in $iE$ preserved by $S_F$. Bochner expectation commutes with
   345	  this bounded compression. The constant columns are retained in the full $F$
   346	  operator path and mean until this compression; they are inactive only on the
   347	  $iE$ inputs. Since $g_\delta\delta^{a/2} = \sqrt\delta$ and $g_\delta > 0$,
   348	  division gives the unscaled covariance
   349	  \begin{equation}\label{E:symplectic-unscaled-covariance}
   350	    \E[M_m(u)W(i_I\Phi)]
   351	    =\delta^{a/2}H_{m,E}(\Phi)(u),\qquad u\le\ell_m .
   352	  \end{equation}
   353	  The factor here is $\delta^{a/2}$, not $\sqrt\delta$. Completion in the
   354	  earlier covariance identity permits every $\Phi \in H_I$, without positivity
   355	  or smoothness.

   357	  The operator $T_mT_m^*$ is the orthogonal projection onto the original
   358	  isometry's closed range. Thus, $W((I-T_mT_m^*)i_I\Phi)$ is orthogonal to the
   359	  entire fast first chaos. Every continuous linear coordinate of $M_m$ is an
   360	  $L^2$ limit of finite $W_m$-basis sums. Its covariance with this difference

   362	  functionals separate its values. Hence,
   363	  \[
   364	    \E[M_m(u)W(i_I\Phi)]
   365	    =\E[M_m(u)W_m(T_m^*i_I\Phi)] .
   366	  \]

   368	  to obtain \eqref{E:symplectic-block-direction} on $[0,\ell_m]$, then stop both
   369	  sides. No unstopped equality beyond $\ell_m$ is asserted.

   375	  $\delta$; all identities are fixed-parameter instances. This proves
   376	  Proposition~\ref{P:symplectic-block-mean}.
   377	\end{proof}

   379	For zero covariance the operator paths and covariance means vanish, and the
   380	claims reduce directly to the free identity in Lemma~\ref{L:symplectic-free}.
   381	These results give a lower bound on the operator norm and its exact completed
   382	mean application. They provide no uniform bound on the control radius,
   383	stochastic moment upper bound or nonlinear product ratio by themselves.
     1	\section{The temporal equilibrium density}
     2	\label{S:temporal-equilibrium}
     3	
     4	We use Euler's function $\Gamma_E(x) = \int_0^\infty u^{x-1}e^{-u}\ud u$, $x >
     5	0$, and $\operatorname{Beta}(x,y) = \int_0^1t^{x-1}(1-t)^{y-1}\ud t$, $x,y > 0$.
     6	Both integrals are positive and finite.
     7	
     8	\begin{lemma}[Gamma and Beta identities]\label{L:equilibrium-gamma-beta}
     9	  For positive arguments,
    10	  \begin{align*}
    11	    \Gamma_E(x+1)&=x\Gamma_E(x),\\
    12	    \operatorname{Beta}(x,y)
    13	    &=\frac{\Gamma_E(x)\Gamma_E(y)}{\Gamma_E(x+y)},\\
    14	    \Gamma_E(2x)
    15	    &=\frac{2^{2x-1}\Gamma_E(x)\Gamma_E(x+1/2)}{\sqrt\pi}.
    16	  \end{align*}
    17	\end{lemma}
    18	
    19	\begin{proof}
    20	  Integration by parts gives the recurrence, with vanishing boundary terms. In
    21	  the positive product Gamma integral, use $(u,v) = (Rt,R(1-t))$, with Jacobian
    22	  $R$; Tonelli gives the Beta--Gamma identity. For the last identity, symmetry,
    23	  then $t = (1+v)/2$ and $v^2 = w$, give $\operatorname{Beta}(x,x) =
    24	  2^{1-2x}\operatorname{Beta}(1/2,x)$. Also $\Gamma_E(1/2) = \int_\R e^{-z^2}\ud
    25	  z = \sqrt\pi$: the substitution $u = z^2$ gives the first equality, and
    26	  squaring the positive Gaussian integral and using polar coordinates gives
    27	  $2\pi\int_0^\infty re^{-r^2}\ud r = \pi$. Substituting these into the
    28	  Beta--Gamma identity proves duplication. This proves
    29	  Lemma~\ref{L:equilibrium-gamma-beta}.
    30	\end{proof}
    31	
    32	\begin{lemma}[Exact potential and mass]\label{L:temporal-equilibrium}
    33	  For $0 < a < 1$ put $r = (1-a)/2$ and, for $0 < t < 1$,
    34	  \begin{equation}\label{E:temporal-equilibrium-density}
    35	    f_a(t)=\frac{[t(1-t)]^{-r}}{\Gamma_E(r)\Gamma_E(1-r)}.
    36	  \end{equation}
    37	  This positive function belongs to $L^1(0,1)\cap L^2(0,1)$, and
    38	  \begin{align}
    39	    \int_0^1|s-t|^{-a}f_a(t)\ud t&=1
    40	    &&\text{for every }s\in[0,1],\label{E:temporal-equilibrium-potential}\\
    41	    M_a:=\int_0^1f_a(t)\ud t
    42	    &=\frac{\Gamma_E((1+a)/2)}
    43	    {\Gamma_E(1+a)\Gamma_E((1-a)/2)}>0.
    44	    \label{E:temporal-equilibrium-mass}
    45	  \end{align}
    46	\end{lemma}
    47	
    48	\begin{proof}
    49	  The positive binomial series $(1-z)^{-p} = \sum_{n\ge0}(p)_nz^n/n!$, $p > 0$,
    50	  $0 \le z < 1$, follows directly as follows. Its coefficient ratio gives
    51	  uniform convergence on compact subintervals, including for its derivative.
    52	  Termwise differentiation gives $(1-z)y' = py$, $y(0) = 1$; hence $(1-z)^py$ is
    53	  constant one. Here $(p)_0 = 1$, $(p)_n = p(p+1)\cdots(p+n-1)$. All terms used
    54	  below are nonnegative, so Tonelli applies.
    55	
    56	  For $0 < s < 1$ split the integral of $|s-t|^{2r-1}[t(1-t)]^{-r}$ into left
    57	  and right parts. In the left part, $t = su$ gives
    58	  \begin{align*}
    59	    L(s)
    60	    &=s^r\int_0^1(1-u)^{2r-1}u^{-r}(1-su)^{-r}\ud u\\
    61	    &=\operatorname{Beta}(1-r,2r)s^r
    62	    \sum_{n\ge0}
    63	    \frac{(r)_n(1-r)_ns^n}{(1+r)_n n!}.
    64	  \end{align*}
    65	  The Beta ratio follows from the Gamma recurrence. Since $(r)_n/(1+r)_n =
    66	  r/(r+n)$, expanding the incomplete Beta integral gives
    67	  \[
    68	    L(s)=r\operatorname{Beta}(1-r,2r)B_s(r,r),\qquad
    69	    B_s(r,r)=\int_0^s u^{r-1}(1-u)^{r-1}\ud u.
    70	  \]
    71	  Reflection makes the right part $L(1-s)$, while symmetry gives
    72	  $B_s(r,r)+B_{1-s}(r,r) = \operatorname{Beta}(r,r)$. The full integral is
    73	  therefore $r\operatorname{Beta}(1-r,2r)\operatorname{Beta}(r,r) =
    74	  \Gamma_E(r)\Gamma_E(1-r)$. All integrals are finite because $-r > -1$ and
    75	  $2r-1 > -1$. At $s = 0$ the integral is directly $\operatorname{Beta}(r,1-r) =
    76	  \Gamma_E(r)\Gamma_E(1-r)$; $s = 1$ follows by reflection. This proves
    77	  \eqref{E:temporal-equilibrium-potential}, including the endpoints without a
    78	  limiting argument there.
    79	
    80	  Integrability and square integrability follow from $-r > -1$ and $-2r = a-1 >
    81	  -1$. Finally,
    82	  \[
    83	    M_a=
    84	    \frac{\operatorname{Beta}(1-r,1-r)}
    85	    {\Gamma_E(r)\Gamma_E(1-r)}
    86	    =\frac{\Gamma_E(1-r)}{\Gamma_E(2-2r)\Gamma_E(r)},
    87	  \]
    88	  which is~\eqref{E:temporal-equilibrium-mass}. Its time mass has not been
    89	  renormalized. This proves Lemma~\ref{L:temporal-equilibrium}.
    90	\end{proof}

    21	\subsection{Global bounds and the unmasked spectral bottom}
    22	
    23	\begin{lemma}[Gaussian envelope for the original covariance]
    24	  \label{L:variational-heat-envelope}
    25	  For the normalized heat kernel $p_\epsilon(x) =
    26	  (2\pi\epsilon)^{-d/2}e^{-|x|^2/(2\epsilon)}$,
    27	  \begin{equation}\label{E:variational-heat-envelope}
    28	    (\Gamma*p_\epsilon)(x)
    29	    =\int e^{i\xi\cdot x}e^{-\epsilon|\xi|^2/2}\mu(\ud\xi),
    30	    \qquad
    31	    0\le(\Gamma*p_\epsilon)(x)
    32	    \le(\Gamma*p_\epsilon)(0)<\infty.
    33	  \end{equation}
    34	  The value at zero is strictly positive.
    35	\end{lemma}
    36	
    37	\begin{proof}
    38	  A positive tempered Radon measure has polynomial ball growth. Indeed, evaluate
    39	  its tempered bound on a nonnegative smooth cutoff equal to one on $B_1$,
    40	  dilated by $R \ge 1$. Its finitely many Schwartz seminorms are bounded by
    41	  $CR^N$, so positivity gives a ball-mass bound $CR^N$. Summing dyadic annuli
    42	  shows that $(1+|x|)^{-L}$ is integrable for $L > N$. Apply this separately to
    43	  $\Gamma$ and $\mu$. Gaussian weights are therefore integrable against both
    44	  measures. The classical convolution on the left is finite and smooth locally
    45	  in $x$: on compact $x$ sets its translated Gaussian derivatives are bounded by
    46	  any fixed sufficiently fast polynomial weight in the integration variable.
    47	
    48	  Pair the convolution with a Schwartz test $\varphi$. Absolute Fubini is
    49	  justified by these weights. The resulting pairing is that of $\Gamma$ with
    50	  $p_\epsilon*\varphi$. Applying the spectral convention in
    51	  Hypothesis~\ref{H:homog} and the identity $\int p_\epsilon(y)e^{-i\xi\cdot
    52	  y}\ud y = e^{-\epsilon|\xi|^2/2}$ gives exactly the right side
    53	  of~\eqref{E:variational-heat-envelope} as a distribution. The heat kernel is
    54	  even, so either Fourier sign gives that same Gaussian multiplier. Its spectral
    55	  integral is absolutely finite and continuous in $x$ by dominated convergence.
    56	  Thus, equality of the two continuous distributions gives equality at every
    57	  $x$, without an extra normalization factor. The physical convolution is
    58	  nonnegative. Evenness of $\mu$ makes the spectral integral real, and its
    59	  absolute value is bounded by its total Gaussian mass, the value at zero.
    60	  Finally, $\Gamma \ne 0$ and $p_\epsilon > 0$ give strict positivity there.
    61	  This proves Lemma~\ref{L:variational-heat-envelope}.
    62	\end{proof}

    64	\begin{lemma}[Global regularity of the original mean]
    65	  \label{L:variational-global-mean}
    66	  Every mixed time and space derivative of $h_s$ is globally bounded in space,
    67	  uniformly on compact time intervals. In particular, for $I = [0,1]$ there are
    68	  finite constants $M,C_\Psi$ such that
    69	  \begin{equation}\label{E:variational-global-mean}
    70	    0\le h_s(x)\le M,\qquad
    71	    \|h_s-h_t\|_\infty\le C_\Psi|s-t|,
    72	    \qquad s,t\in I.
    73	  \end{equation}
    74	\end{lemma}
    75	
    76	\begin{proof}
    77	  Extend $\Psi$ by zero in time; its compact support inside $(0,1)$ makes this a
    78	  smooth extension. For any mixed derivative $D\Psi$, a fixed $\epsilon > 0$ and
    79	  compactness of its common spatial support give $|D\Psi(t,x)| \le
    80	  C_Dp_\epsilon(x)$ for all $t,x$. Here the heat kernel has a positive minimum
    81	  on that support. Lemma~\ref{L:variational-heat-envelope} consequently bounds
    82	  $\Gamma*|D\Psi(t,\cdot)|$ uniformly in $t,x$. Ordinary local differentiation
    83	  against the Radon measure gives the corresponding derivatives of the
    84	  convolution. After the change $r = s-t$,
    85	  \[
    86	    h_s(x)=\int_\R |r|^{-a}
    87	    (\Gamma*\Psi(s-r,\cdot))(x)\ud r.
    88	  \]
    89	  For $s$ in a compact interval the relevant $r$ lie in a fixed bounded
    90	  interval. The preceding global bound times $|r|^{-a}$ is integrable since $a <
    91	  1$. Every derivative thus falls on the smooth test and passes through the
    92	  integral by dominated convergence, with the claimed global spatial bounds.
    93	  Nonnegativity follows from positive kernels. The bounded time derivative
    94	  proves the Lipschitz estimate. No directional decay of the mean has been
    95	  inferred. This proves Lemma~\ref{L:variational-global-mean}.
    96	\end{proof}

    98	\begin{proposition}[The unmasked Rayleigh rate]
    99	  \label{P:variational-unmasked-rate}
   100	  On complex $L^2(\R^d)$, the operator $H_s = -\Delta-h_s$ is self-adjoint on
   101	  $H^2$, with form domain $H^1$ and form $q_s(f) = \|\nabla f\|_2^2-\int
   102	  h_s|f|^2$. Its spectral bottom $E_s$ is uniformly negative on $I$. The
   103	  positive rate $\lambda_{\Psi,s} = \sqrt{-E_s}$ satisfies
   104	  \begin{equation}\label{E:variational-real-rayleigh}
   105	    \lambda_{\Psi,s}^2
   106	    =\sup_{\substack{f\in H^1(\R^d;\R)\\\|f\|_2=1}}
   107	    \left(\int h_sf^2-\|\nabla f\|_2^2\right).
   108	  \end{equation}
   109	  It is Lipschitz on $I$, and $I_\Psi: = \int_0^1\lambda_{\Psi,s}\ud s$ is
   110	  positive and finite. No eigenstate at the unmasked bottom is asserted.
   111	\end{proposition}
   112	
   113	\begin{proof}
   114	  The Fourier Laplacian $A = -\Delta$ is self-adjoint on $H^2$, being
   115	  multiplication by $|\xi|^2$ with its maximal domain. Multiplication $B_s =
   116	  -h_s$ is bounded self-adjoint with norm at most $M$. Thus, $H_s = A+B_s$ is
   117	  densely defined, symmetric and closed on $H^2$; the two graph norms are
   118	  equivalent under a bounded perturbation. For real $b > M$,
   119	  \[
   120	    H_s-ib=(I+B_s(A-ib)^{-1})(A-ib).
   121	  \]
   122	  The first factor has a Neumann inverse because $\|B_s(A-ib)^{-1}\| \le M/b <
   123	  1$, and the same holds with $+ib$. To check self-adjointness directly, for $u
   124	  \in D(H_s^*)$ solve $(H_s-ib)v = (H_s^*-ib)u$ with $v \in D(H_s)$. Then $u-v
   125	  \in \ker(H_s^*-ib) = \operatorname{Ran}(H_s+ib)^\perp = \{0\}$. Hence,
   126	  $D(H_s^*) = D(H_s)$.
   127	
   128	  Set $c_{\mathrm{shift}} = 1+M$ and $J_s = H_s+c_{\mathrm{shift}} \ge 1$.
   129	  Integration by parts on $H^2$ gives
   130	  \[
   131	    \|J_s^{1/2}f\|_2^2=q_s(f)+c_{\mathrm{shift}}\|f\|_2^2,\qquad
   132	    \|f\|_{H^1}^2\le\|J_s^{1/2}f\|_2^2
   133	    \le c_{\mathrm{shift}}\|f\|_{H^1}^2.
   134	  \]
   135	  Spectral cutoffs $1_{[1,n]}(J_s)$ show that $H^2 = D(J_s)$ is a core for the
   136	  half-power norm; Fourier cutoffs give its density in $H^1$. Completion in the
   137	  equivalent norms identifies $D(J_s^{1/2})$ and $H^1$ as $L^2$ subspaces, since
   138	  both norms dominate $L^2$. This proves the stated form domain.
   139	
   140	  The spectral lower bound gives one direction of the Rayleigh identity. For the
   141	  reverse, nonzero spectral projections in $[E_s,E_s+\epsilon]$ give unit $H^2$
   142	  vectors with Rayleigh values at most $E_s+\epsilon$. The bottom is finite
   143	  because the operator is bounded below and has finite Rayleigh tests. Let
   144	  $\epsilon\downarrow0$. Real tests give the same infimum: $q_s(u+iv) =
   145	  q_s(u)+q_s(v)$, so the quotient is the norm-weighted average of the nonzero
   146	  real quotients. This proves the Rayleigh identity with $-E_s$ on the left. The
   147	  following negative upper bound justifies writing that value as
   148	  $\lambda_{\Psi,s}^2$ in~\eqref{E:variational-real-rayleigh}.
   149	
   150	  Proposition~\ref{P:compact-original-common-trial} supplies, for this original
   151	  $\Psi$, one unit compactly supported $w$ and a finite plateau mask with a
   152	  common strictly negative upper bound $\epsilon_0 > 0$. Its trial has support
   153	  in $B_{2L}$; choose its plateau radius $R_0 \ge 2L$. The unmasked form on this
   154	  same $w$ is no larger. Consequently, $-M \le E_s \le -\epsilon_0 < 0$, and
   155	  $\sqrt{\epsilon_0} \le \lambda_{\Psi,s} \le \sqrt M$. Comparing identical unit
   156	  form tests gives $|E_s-E_t| \le \|h_s-h_t\|_\infty$ and therefore
   157	  \[
   158	    |\lambda_{\Psi,s}-\lambda_{\Psi,t}|
   159	    \le \frac{C_\Psi}{2\sqrt{\epsilon_0}}|s-t|.
   160	  \]
   161	  This also proves positivity and finiteness of $I_\Psi$. No compact-potential
   162	  spectral theorem was applied to $H_s$. This proves
   163	  Proposition~\ref{P:variational-unmasked-rate}.
   164	\end{proof}

   166	\subsection{Removing masks from the numerical lower rate}
   167	
   168	\begin{proposition}[Monotone rates and the original point moment]
   169	  \label{P:variational-remove-mask}
   170	  There is an increasing family of admissible radial masks $m_R$ tending to one,
   171	  for which the compact ground rates satisfy
   172	  $\lambda_{R,s}\uparrow\lambda_{\Psi,s}$ uniformly on $I$ as $R \to \infty$,
   173	  with the compact ground statements used for $R \ge R_0(\Psi)$. For the
   174	  original canonical solution and any fixed $x$,
   175	  \begin{equation}\label{E:variational-unmasked-point-lower}
   176	    \liminf_{T\to\infty}T^{-\kappa}\log\E|u(T,x)|^2
   177	    \ge2I_\Psi-\frac{v_\Psi}{2}.
   178	  \end{equation}
   179	\end{proposition}
   180	
   181	\begin{proof}
   182	  Put $F(t) = e^{-1/t}$ for $t > 0$ and zero otherwise, and define
   183	  \[
   184	    \chi(r)=\frac{F(2-r)}{F(2-r)+F(r-1)},\qquad
   185	    m_R(x)=\chi(|x|/R).
   186	  \]
   187	  The denominator is positive. The numerator decreases and the second
   188	  denominator term increases; thus $\chi$ is nonincreasing, equals one on $r \le
   189	  1$, and zero on $r \ge 2$. Flatness of $F$ at zero gives smoothness. Since
   190	  $\chi$ is constant near zero, $m_R$ is smooth also at the spatial origin.
   191	  These even $[0,1]$ masks increase pointwise to one.
   192	
   193	  Choose $R_0$ so the preceding common trial lies in the plateau. Every $R \ge
   194	  R_0$ has the same negative margin. For each fixed $R$, the compact-family
   195	  theorem applies to $m_Rh_s$. Its real Rayleigh formula follows from the same
   196	  real/complex quotient argument as~\eqref{E:variational-real-rayleigh}. The
   197	  rates are continuous, positive, at most $\sqrt M$ and monotone in $R$. For
   198	  every fixed real unit $f \in H^1$, dominated convergence gives $\int m_Rh_sf^2
   199	  \to \int h_sf^2$. Hence,
   200	  \[
   201	    \sup_{R\ge R_0}\lambda_{R,s}^2
   202	    =\sup_{\|f\|_2=1,\ f\in H^1(\R^d;\R)}
   203	    \sup_{R\ge R_0}
   204	    \left(\int m_Rh_sf^2-\|\nabla f\|_2^2\right)
   205	    =\lambda_{\Psi,s}^2.
   206	  \]
   207	  Only two numerical suprema were interchanged. Positive square roots give the
   208	  pointwise rate convergence. For $R_n = R_0+n$ and $\epsilon > 0$, the
   209	  increasing open sets $\{s:\lambda_{\Psi,s}-\lambda_{R_n,s}<\epsilon\}$ cover
   210	  compact $I$. A finite subcover lies in the largest one, proving uniform
   211	  convergence. Monotonicity extends it to all real $R \to \infty$. Therefore,
   212	  $\int_I\lambda_{R,s}\ud s\uparrow I_\Psi$.
   213	
   214	  At each fixed $R$ use this very same mask in the operator path and mean when
   215	  applying Proposition~\ref{P:raw-block-original-lower}. It gives the lower
   216	  bound with $2\int_I\lambda_{R,s}\ud s-v_\Psi/2$ for the same original point
   217	  liminf. Taking the numerical supremum over these individual bounds proves
   218	  \eqref{E:variational-unmasked-point-lower}. There is no $R(T)$, unmasked noisy
   219	  wave, uniform-in-mask Gaussian estimate or exchange of source and time limits.
   220	  This proves Proposition~\ref{P:variational-remove-mask}.
   221	\end{proof}

   223	\subsection{Full-class dilation and finite variational values for nonnegative controls}
   224	
   225	\begin{lemma}[Radon and Rayleigh dilation]\label{L:variational-control-dilation}
   226	  For $r > 0$ the map
   227	  \begin{equation}\label{E:variational-control-dilation}
   228	    (D_r\Psi)(s,x)=r^{d+2-\alpha}\Psi(s,rx)
   229	  \end{equation}
   230	  is a bijection of $\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{pos}}$, with inverse $D_{1/r}$. With
   231	  the same original covariance,
   232	  \begin{equation}\label{E:variational-dilation-values}
   233	    h_{D_r\Psi,s}(x)=r^2h_{\Psi,s}(rx),\qquad
   234	    v_{D_r\Psi}=r^{4-\alpha}v_\Psi,\qquad
   235	    \lambda_{D_r\Psi,s}=r\lambda_{\Psi,s},\quad
   236	    I_{D_r\Psi}=rI_\Psi.
   237	  \end{equation}
   238	\end{lemma}
   239	
   240	\begin{proof}
   241	  Positive dilation preserves the full smooth positive nonzero class;
   242	  multiplication of its amplitude powers gives the stated inverse. Homogeneity
   243	  of the physical Radon measure gives, for every nonnegative measurable $G$,
   244	  \[
   245	    \int G(ry)\Gamma(\ud y)
   246	    =r^{\alpha-d}\int G(z)\Gamma(\ud z).
   247	  \]
   248	  Indeed, its left pushforward measure on a Borel set $A$ is $\Gamma(A/r) =
   249	  r^{\alpha-d}\Gamma(A)$. Positive Tonelli applies this identity inside the
   250	  temporal convolution, giving $h_{D_r\Psi,s}(x) = r^2h_{\Psi,s}(rx)$. Now use
   251	  the \emph{Lebesgue} substitution $z = rx$ in the original pairing:
   252	  \[
   253	    v_{D_r\Psi}=r^{d+2-\alpha}r^2r^{-d}v_\Psi
   254	    =r^{4-\alpha}v_\Psi.
   255	  \]
   256	  This distinguishes the Radon pushforward from the spatial volume factor; it
   257	  includes singular covariances and white noise.
   258	
   259	  The map $U_rf(x) = r^{d/2}f(rx)$ is a unitary bijection on real $L^2$,
   260	  preserving $H^1,H^2$ as sets under its inverse. Weak derivatives give
   261	  $\|\nabla U_rf\|_2^2 = r^2\|\nabla f\|_2^2$ and $\int h_{D_r\Psi,s}(U_rf)^2 =
   262	  r^2\int h_{\Psi,s}f^2$. The real Rayleigh bijection proves the squared rate
   263	  identity; the rates are positive, so their square roots and integrals give
   264	  \eqref{E:variational-dilation-values}. On $H^2$ this is also $H_{D_r\Psi,s}U_r
   265	  = r^2U_rH_{\Psi,s}$. Time has not been rescaled. For compact masks the
   266	  corresponding identity uses $m_R(rx) = m_{R/r}(x)$; a fixed mask radius is not
   267	  invariant. This proves Lemma~\ref{L:variational-control-dilation}.
   268	\end{proof}

   270	\begin{proposition}[Intrinsic variational lower bounds]
   271	  \label{P:variational-positive-scores}
   272	  For $c > 0$, the set of variational values
   273	  $\{cI_\Psi-v_\Psi/2:\Psi\in\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{pos}}\}$ is nonempty and
   274	  bounded above. Its finite real supremum $S_c^{\mathrm{pos}}$ is positive and
   275	  satisfies
   276	  \begin{equation}\label{E:variational-score-homogeneity}
   277	    S_c^{\mathrm{pos}}=c^{(4-\alpha)/(3-\alpha)}S_1^{\mathrm{pos}},
   278	    \qquad
   279	    Q_2\ge S_2^{\mathrm{pos}},
   280	  \end{equation}
   281	  where $Q_2$ is the original point liminf. The coefficient-one value is an
   282	  auxiliary variational value; no first-moment or source-constant identification
   283	  is asserted.
   284	\end{proposition}
   285	
   286	\begin{proof}
   287	  Write $k = 3-\alpha > 0$, $q = 4-\alpha = k+1$ and $m = q/k > 1$. Fix one
   288	  $\Psi_0$ from the nonempty class and put $I_0 = I_{\Psi_0} > 0$, $v_0 =
   289	  v_{\Psi_0} > 0$. Positivity of the latter is
   290	  Lemma~\ref{L:compact-raw-profile}. For $r_0 = (I_0/v_0)^{1/k} > 0$, which need
   291	  not be less than one, the exact real-power identity gives
   292	  \[
   293	    I_{D_{r_0}\Psi_0}-v_{D_{r_0}\Psi_0}/2
   294	    =r_0I_0-r_0^qv_0/2=r_0I_0/2>0.
   295	  \]
   296	  This positive value is obtained from a smooth nonnegative control.
   297	
   298	  For $c > 0$ put $r_c = c^{1/k}$ and $K_c = c^m > 0$.
   299	  Lemma~\ref{L:variational-control-dilation} and the exact scalar powers give,
   300	  for every $\Psi$,
   301	  \begin{equation}\label{E:variational-score-set-scaling}
   302	    cI_{D_{r_c}\Psi}-v_{D_{r_c}\Psi}/2
   303	    =K_c(I_\Psi-v_\Psi/2).
   304	  \end{equation}
   305	  Since $D_{r_c}$ is a bijection of the entire class, the whole set of
   306	  variational values with coefficient $c$ is $K_c$ times the whole
   307	  coefficient-one set of variational values.
   308	
   309	  We prove boundedness before taking finite-real suprema. The independent
   310	  Theorem~\ref{T:full-upper}, for the \emph{same canonical solution}, gives
   311	  \[
   312	    \E|u(T,0)|^2\le e(T+2)^d e^{C_{\mathrm{up}}T^\kappa},
   313	    \qquad T\ge1,\quad C_{\mathrm{up}}<\infty.
   314	  \]
   315	  Its prefactor is negligible: choose $\epsilon = \kappa/2 > 0$, use $\log T \le
   316	  (T^\epsilon-1)/\epsilon$ and $\log(T+2) \le \log T+\log3$ for $T \ge 1$, and
   317	  divide by $T^\kappa$. Thus, the original point limsup is at most
   318	  $C_{\mathrm{up}}$. One fixed test/mask lower bound gives a finite lower bound
   319	  for $Q_2$, so $Q_2$ is finite. By~\eqref{E:variational-unmasked-point-lower}
   320	  every coefficient-two variational expression is at most this same $Q_2 \le
   321	  C_{\mathrm{up}}$, uniformly in $\Psi$.
   322	  Equation~\eqref{E:variational-score-set-scaling} at $c = 2$ consequently
   323	  bounds all coefficient-one variational values by $C_{\mathrm{up}}/K_2$. The
   324	  nonempty set has a finite real supremum $S_1^{\mathrm{pos}} > 0$ by the
   325	  positive test above.
   326	
   327	  For general $c$, set equality and $K_c > 0$ show that $K_cS_1^{\mathrm{pos}}$
   328	  is the supremum: it is an upper bound, and every smaller number is exceeded by
   329	  $K_c$ times a coefficient-one variational expression within the corresponding
   330	  positive distance of its supremum. This proves finiteness, positivity and the
   331	  first identity in~\eqref{E:variational-score-homogeneity}. Taking the
   332	  numerical supremum of the coefficient-two lower bounds proves the second.
   333	  Although $2^m > 2$, the resulting $S_2^{\mathrm{pos}} > 2S_1^{\mathrm{pos}}$
   334	  is only a comparison of auxiliary variational values. It is not a Jensen
   335	  improvement without a first-moment identification. This proves
   336	  Proposition~\ref{P:variational-positive-scores}.
   337	\end{proof}
   338	
   339	For $\Gamma = 0$, the mean, original variance and Rayleigh rate are zero. Set

   341	the corresponding zero moment rate. Strict positivity above is restricted to

    22	\subsection{A scalar row estimate for a measure}
    23	
    24	Let $\nu$ be a positive Radon measure satisfying
    25	\begin{equation}\label{E:frequency-translated-growth}
    26	  \nu(B(y,r)) \le C r^\alpha,
    27	  \qquad y \in \R^d,\quad r > 0,
    28	\end{equation}
    29	where $C \ge 0$. If the estimate is initially known for open balls, apply it at
    30	radius $r+\epsilon$ and let $\epsilon \downarrow 0$ to obtain the closed-ball
    31	estimate. Neither evenness nor a density is assumed here.
    32	Using~\eqref{E:masked-frequency-pair}, define
    33	\begin{align}
    34	  \Phi_h(\xi,\eta)
    35	  &:= \frac{\mathcal{Q}_h(|\xi|,|\eta|)}
    36	  {\langle\xi\rangle\langle\eta\rangle},
    37	  \label{E:frequency-row-kernel}\\
    38	  J_h(\xi)
    39	  &:= \langle\xi\rangle^{2\gamma}
    40	  \int_{\R^d}\Phi_h(\xi,\xi-\lambda)\nu(\ud\lambda).
    41	  \label{E:frequency-row-integral}
    42	\end{align}
    43	These are initially nonnegative extended integrals. In particular, the notation
    44	denotes a pushforward of $\nu$, not integration against an assumed spectral
    45	density.
    46	
    47	\begin{proposition}[Uniform scalar row]\label{P:frequency-row}
    48	  There is a finite $K = K(\alpha,a,\gamma)$, independent of $d,\nu,C,h$ and
    49	  $\xi$, such that
    50	  \begin{equation}\label{E:frequency-row-bound}
    51	    \sup_{\xi\in\R^d}J_h(\xi) \le K C B_\alpha(h),
    52	    \qquad 0 < h \le 1.
    53	  \end{equation}
    54	\end{proposition}
    55	
    56	\begin{proof}
    57	  If $C = 0$, a countable covering by finite balls gives $\nu = 0$, and the
    58	  result is immediate. Suppose $C > 0$. For each $\xi$, let $\nu_\xi$ be the
    59	  pushforward under $\lambda \mapsto \eta = \xi-\lambda$. Then $\nu_\xi(B(0,R))
    60	  \le CR^\alpha$. For $q \ge 1$, put
    61	  \[
    62	    A_\xi(q) = \int_{|\eta|\le5q}\langle\eta\rangle^{-1}
    63	    \nu_\xi(\ud\eta).
    64	  \]
    65	  Choose $N = \lceil\log_2(5q)\rceil$, so $5q \le 2^N < 10q$. Splitting into the
    66	  unit ball and the annuli $2^j < |\eta| \le 2^{j+1}$ gives
    67	  \[
    68	    A_\xi(q) \le C\left(1+2^\alpha
    69	    \sum_{j=0}^{N-1}2^{j(\alpha-1)}\right).
    70	  \]
    71	  The geometric sum is bounded when $\alpha < 1$, is $N$ when $\alpha = 1$, and
    72	  is at most $2^{N(\alpha-1)}/(2^{\alpha-1}-1)$ when $\alpha > 1$. Hence,
    73	  \begin{equation}\label{E:frequency-inverse-bessel}
    74	    A_\xi(q) \le K_\alpha C
    75	    \begin{cases}
    76	      1, & \alpha < 1,\\
    77	      1+\log q, & \alpha = 1,\\
    78	      q^{\alpha-1}, & \alpha > 1,
    79	    \end{cases}
    80	  \end{equation}
    81	  with a constant depending only on $\alpha$.
    82	
    83	  Set $q = \max(1,|\xi|)$ and $\epsilon = 1-2\gamma > 0$. On $|\lambda| \le 4q$
    84	  we have $|\eta| \le 5q$. Both bracket powers in $\mathcal{Q}_h$ are at most
    85	  one, since $a-1 < 0$. The contribution of this region to $J_h(\xi)$ is at most
    86	  \[
    87	    2\langle\xi\rangle^{-\epsilon}A_\xi(q)
    88	    \le 2q^{-\epsilon}A_\xi(q).
    89	  \]
    90	  If $\alpha < 1$, this is uniformly bounded
    91	  by~\eqref{E:frequency-inverse-bessel}. If $\alpha = 1$, the bound follows from
    92	  \[
    93	    e^{-\epsilon u}(1+u) \le 1+\frac1{e\epsilon},
    94	    \qquad u = \log q \ge 0,
    95	  \]
    96	  since $u e^{-\epsilon u}$ has maximum $1/(e\epsilon)$. If $\alpha > 1$, the
    97	  remaining power is $q^{\alpha+2\gamma-2}$, whose exponent is negative
    98	  by~\eqref{E:variance-gamma-range}. Thus, the near contribution is at most a
    99	  constant times $C$ in all three cases.
   100	
   101	  On the far region write $r = |\lambda| > 4q$. Then
   102	  \[
   103	    |\eta| \ge \frac{3r}4,\qquad
   104	    \big||\eta|-|\xi|\big| \ge \frac r2,\qquad
   105	    |\eta|+|\xi| \ge \frac r2.
   106	  \]
   107	  Each oscillatory bracket is at least $\langle hr\rangle/2$, whereas
   108	  $\langle\eta\rangle^{-1} \le 4/(3r)$ and $\langle\xi\rangle^{-\epsilon} \le
   109	  1$. Consequently, the far contribution is at most
   110	  \[
   111	    \frac43\,2^{2-a}\int_{|\lambda|>4q}
   112	    |\lambda|^{-1}\langle h|\lambda|\rangle^{a-1}\nu(\ud\lambda).
   113	  \]
   114	  Enlarge the domain to $|\lambda| > 1$ and split it into dyadic annuli.
   115	  Applying~\eqref{E:frequency-translated-growth} to their masses bounds this
   116	  expression by a constant depending only on $\alpha,a$ times $C S(h)$, where
   117	  \[
   118	    S(h) = \sum_{j=0}^\infty
   119	    2^{j(\alpha-1)}\langle h2^j\rangle^{a-1}.
   120	  \]
   121	  Choose $L = \lfloor\log_2(1/h)\rfloor \ge 0$. For $j \le L$ the bracket power
   122	  is at most one. For $j \ge L+1$ it is at most $(h2^j)^{a-1}$. Since
   123	  $\alpha+a-2 < 0$, the tail is
   124	  \[
   125	    \frac{h^{a-1}2^{(L+1)(\alpha+a-2)}}{1-2^{\alpha+a-2}}
   126	    \le \frac{h^{1-\alpha}}{1-2^{\alpha+a-2}}.
   127	  \]
   128	  The inequality uses $2^{L+1} > 1/h$ and the negative exponent. The finite sum
   129	  is bounded by $1/(1-2^{\alpha-1})$ for $\alpha < 1$, by $1+\log_2(1/h)$ for
   130	  $\alpha = 1$, and by
   131	  \[
   132	    \frac{2^{\alpha-1}h^{1-\alpha}}{2^{\alpha-1}-1}
   133	  \]
   134	  for $\alpha > 1$. Since $h^{1-\alpha} \le 1$ in the first case, we obtain
   135	  $S(h) \le K_{\alpha,a}B_\alpha(h)$. Combining the near and far bounds, and
   136	  using $B_\alpha(h) \ge 1$, proves the assertion and finiteness of the original
   137	  integral. All constants arose from numerical shell estimates and are
   138	  independent of $d$. This proves Proposition~\ref{P:frequency-row}.
   139	\end{proof}

   141	\begin{corollary}[A time exponent above one half]\label{C:frequency-time}
   142	  For every
   143	  \begin{equation}\label{E:variance-beta-range}
   144	    \frac12 < \beta < \min\left(1-\frac a2,
   145	    \frac{3-a-\alpha}{2}\right),
   146	  \end{equation}
   147	  there is a finite $K_\beta = K_\beta(\alpha,a,\gamma,\beta)$ such that
   148	  \begin{equation}\label{E:frequency-time-bound}
   149	    h^{2-a}\sup_\xi J_h(\xi) \le K_\beta C h^{2\beta},
   150	    \qquad 0 < h \le 1.
   151	  \end{equation}
   152	\end{corollary}
   153	
   154	\begin{proof}
   155	  Both upper endpoints in~\eqref{E:variance-beta-range} exceed one half, by $a <
   156	  1$ and $\alpha+a < 2$. If $\alpha < 1$, use $2-a > 2\beta$ in
   157	  Proposition~\ref{P:frequency-row}. If $\alpha > 1$, use $3-a-\alpha > 2\beta$.
   158	  For $\alpha = 1$, set $\delta = 2-a-2\beta > 0$ and $u = \log(1/h)$. Then
   159	  \[
   160	    h^\delta(1+\log(1/h))
   161	    = e^{-\delta u}(1+u) \le 1+\frac1{e\delta}.
   162	  \]
   163	  This absorbs the critical logarithm. No endpoint value of $\beta$ is used.
   164	  This proves Corollary~\ref{C:frequency-time}.
   165	\end{proof}
